articles.title: Trump turns to smoke and mirrors
articles.body:
Trump turns to smoke and mirrors
The US president amplifies distorted claims about Qalibaf on Truth Social, using media fabrications to obscure the setbacks of his war on Iran
TEHRAN — President Donald Trump has turned to psychological warfare and media fabrications in a desperate attempt to distract from the failure of the US military and economic war against Iran.
Such underhanded attempts became even more apparent after Trump reposted a link on Truth Social from the US conservative news outlet Newsmax, which grossly distorted comments made by Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf during his recent diplomatic trip to Iraq.
Newsmax sensationalized the story under the title "Iran Parliament Speaker: 'We Are Hungry, We Cannot Survive,'" attempting to cook up a false narrative of Iranian vulnerability by deliberately twisting Qalibaf’s words. Misquoting the Iranian Parliament speaker, the outlet wrote that no matter how strong military power becomes, if people are hungry, they will not be able to endure. Western outlets immediately spun the story to suggest that Iran is on the verge of collapse and that the US war against Iran, coupled with Washington’s unrelenting economic pressure, could bring down the Islamic Republic.
Nonetheless, a look at Qalibaf’s actual speech delivered in Persian tells a completely different story and sheds light on what was truly said. In a high-level meeting with Iraqi and Iranian economic activists, Qalibaf spoke strategically about the vital need for sovereign nations to maintain both military and economic strength. In this section of his address, the Parliament speaker stressed that alongside formidable military power, economic growth, robust domestic production, and dynamic financial activity are essential pillars to maintaining a country’s overall strength and national resilience. He emphasized that military power alone cannot guarantee a country’s long-term survival if the domestic economy is neglected. In fact, Qalibaf firmly believes that alongside continuously strengthening its defense capabilities, Iran must also bolster its economic foundation and overcome its internal financial challenges precisely to withstand hostile foreign economic pressure.
The media deception occurs against the backdrop of the aggressive US-Israeli war launched on February 28, a joint assault intended to cripple the Islamic Republic that ultimately backfired on its aggressors. When launching the operation, Trump openly declared an intent to force regime change, directly telling the Iranian population to take over their government. Yet, far from achieving its maximalist objectives or collapsing the government, the conflict resulted in the rapid depletion of the US military arsenal, exposing the logistical limits and strategic overreach of American hegemony.
Detailed technical assessments and reports from major American military outlets confirm that months of high-intensity operations have severely drained US weapons stocks—expending nearly two-thirds of its Patriot air defense interceptor inventory, roughly 40 percent of its THAAD interceptors, and a third of its Tomahawk cruise missile supply, while virtually exhausting its precision strike ballistic missiles like ATACMS and PrSM. American military analysts have been forced to admit that Washington simply lacks the industrial manufacturing pace to replenish these advanced systems, proving that claims of having completely wiped out Iranian military power are detached from reality. Iranian military officials have repeatedly dismissed these US proclamations, noting that Iran's defense apparatus remains fully operational, integrated, and capable of sustained deterrence.
Despite these clear tactical setbacks, Trump has continued to operate under extreme geopolitical delusions. Chief among them is his absurd, repeated assertion that the Strait of Hormuz—one of the world's most vital maritime choke points—is now sovereign American territory. Trump has publicly voiced this bizarre claim at least three times. He first floated the idea to a campaign crowd in Long Island, saying that after defeating Iran, he would declare the Strait a territory of the United States. He then doubled down during a press interaction at Joint Base Andrews, claiming the US possessed total control over the region and treated it as American ground. Shortly after, he amplified the delusion by sharing maps on Truth Social depicting the international waterway explicitly tagged as new US territory.
Iranian officials and regional observers were quick to point out the unhinged nature of these statements. Officials in Tehran noted that the vast distance between Washington's military capability and its land-grab fantasies exposes the White House's complete detachment from realities on the ground. The Strait remains an international waterway bordered by sovereign nations, and no amount of Truth Social posts can grant Washington legal or physical ownership over foreign territorial waters.
Trump's unfulfilled claims extend directly to his cycle of military threats, which have repeatedly collapsed into abrupt strategic retreats. This recurring pattern has become so glaring that analysts, financial markets, and international media outlets now widely refer to it as the TACO pattern, an acronym for "Trump Always Chickens Out". Time and again, Trump has issued dramatic ultimatums—threatening to bomb Iranian power plants, target critical energy infrastructure on Kharg Island, or send the country back to the Stone Age if his demands were not met within tight deadlines. Yet every single time the deadline expired and Tehran refused to submit, Trump backed away, offering unilateral extensions, claiming a deal was near, or citing requests from foreign leaders to pause military action.
Having failed to secure a decisive victory on the battlefield, facing a depleted arsenal, and caught in a cycle of empty threats, Washington attempted to shift its focus back to financial strangulation. Trump orchestrated an "economic D-Day" plan against Iran—an aggressive economic warfare operation aimed at crushing the nation’s commercial lifelines and starving its people into submission.
Yet, as Iran’s steadfast endurance neutralizes these hostile measures, Trump’s declared "economic D-Day" has crumbled into another total failure, exposing the utter limits of American coercive leverage. Facing structural defeat on both the military and financial fronts, the White House has resorted to a classic plan to divide and rule—using media fabrications, psychological manipulations on Truth Social, and false narratives about figures like Qalibaf to sow division and disguise Washington's growing impotence on the global stage.

articles.title: Ukraine faces €23B defense funding hole as Western cash lags
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomes international leaders upon their arrival for a coalition of the willing meeting in Kyiv on Aug. 24, 2026. | Pool photo by Henry Nicholls via AFP/Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine faces a €23 billion hole in its defense budget this year, leaving Kyiv scrambling for cash to fight Russia even as Western leaders gathered in the capital to mark the country's independence day and pledge ongoing support.
The money is needed not only for weapons and air defense, but also to pay soldiers, support the families of those killed and ensure Ukraine has the supplies it needs to start 2027.
“We are not asking [you] to fight for us. Give Ukraine everything to stop this war, to stop it faster than Putin can start the next one,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a speech Monday.
Advertisement
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was in Kyiv Monday for a meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing.
European Council President António Costa, Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Estonian President Alar Karis, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and other Nordic and Baltic leaders also attended in person, while French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz joined remotely.
“Ukrainian people deserve not just continued support but our gratitude ... I am determined we [the coalition of the willing] will work together to deliver the support you need,” Burnham said in a statement.
The funding gap originated after the defense ministry brought forward spending originally planned for the second half of the year, while the EU’s €90 billion loan was delayed by roadblocks from Hungary.
“At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half," Zelenskyy said during a meeting with reporters on Saturday. The shortfall comes on top of €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan.
Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June.
Advertisement
"Now, in the second half of the year, those funds need to be compensated for and supplemented,” Zelenskyy added.
The European Commission offered some relief Monday, approving €6.1 billion in new defense procurement for Ukraine. This latest disbursement from the EU’s €90 billion loan package will fund air-defense missiles and ammunition, as well as radars — among Kyiv’s most urgent needs. But the money falls far short of what Ukraine says it requires.
Ukraine needs about €6.8 billion to €8.5 billion to ensure a “normal start” to next year, the Ukrainian leader said. That money is effectively needed in advance to pay for weapons and other supplies for January 2027. Around €17 billion more is needed for military salaries, payments to the families of fallen soldiers and other expenses.
“A lot of money is needed,” he added.
But domestic politics are also creating obstacles to international funding. Zelenskyy admitted that Ukrainian lawmakers are stalling the implementation of reforms on which some international aid is conditional.
Overall, parliament is currently delaying 24 reform bills tied to Western funding disbursement. While not all the funds are tied to defense spending, getting EU money would free up Ukraine's scarce resources for other urgent defense needs.
Advertisement
Last week, the Ukrainian parliament’s law enforcement committee removed five government and judicial reform bills from consideration because they are no longer relevant, Ukrainian MP Anastasiya Radina said last week.
Maksym Buzhanskiy, a lawmaker from Zelenskyy's party, defended the committee's decision to remove the bills, claiming they do not correspond to Ukraine commitments needed for EU funding.
Zelenskyy is planning to ask for disbursement of EU funds ahead of schedule.
“I am working on this with the French and the Germans. Practically, we need to bring forward the second portion of the European funds allocated for Ukraine, and this is an extremely difficult task,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Putin adviser raises attacks on British drone factories
articles.body:
An adviser to President Putin has said British factories producing drones for Ukraine could be attacked by what he called unknown sources, as part of a possible Russian response to UK military support for Kyiv, in an interview with BBC Newsnight.
Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian deputy foreign minister who advises the Kremlin, was speaking to Adam Fleming on the programme on Monday. Asked what a semi-military response might involve, he said: “For example, something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine, etc, etc.”
Pressed on whether he meant British factories in Britain being attacked militarily by Russia, he said: “They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources.”
Fedorov said pressure was building on Putin to act against the United Kingdom, telling the programme: “There’s a very serious political and public pressure on President Putin today, to undertake certain measures against UK, because he is considering UK as part of the war in Ukraine, and assistance from the UK is considered as a direct involvement of UK in this war.”
Asked where that pressure came from, he said: “It’s coming from the public opinion polls, it’s coming from journalists, from mass media, it is coming from military. And UK, of course, as considered in the context of Ukraine, is evil Number 1.”
He said Putin had described current developments as the opening of Pandora’s box, and that there had been a very negative reaction in the Kremlin.
On what form a response might take, Fedorov told the programme: “In the coming future we will face a new stage of escalation, in the Ukrainian conflict, and sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK.”
He said the options under discussion included a technical reaction, possibly a hacker attack from an unofficial source, along with political steps, and that he could not entirely exclude something semi-military.
Asked whether he personally would be content with such an attack, he said he would not, adding: “The problem is that we are now facing, in front of the danger, that Ukrainian conflict will be beyond Ukrainian borders. And remembering that UK is a member of NATO, and UK is a nuclear state, the risk is, of course, much higher than it was before, even a couple of months ago.”
Challenged on how such an attack could be justified under international law, he said: “Frankly speaking, who cares today about international law?” He said many in Russian society believed the president had waited too long to answer the UK.
On cyber targets, he said a hacker attack would be directed at a specific enterprise or system rather than broadly, and confirmed when asked that this would mean something governmental, security or military related, “especially to production of the drones or some components for Storm Shadow missiles.”
Fedorov linked the Kremlin’s assessment directly to the transfer of missile blueprints, saying the step meant that from Moscow’s point of view Britain was much more involved, and that a system capable of producing missiles, whether Storm Shadow or a Ukrainian modification, would be considerably more effective than what came before.
He described Moscow as considering the actions of the British Prime Minister as direct military involvement in the conflict.
On the domestic picture, Fedorov acknowledged that fuel queues and Ukrainian strikes on warehouses, including those belonging to the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon, were having an effect, but said he could not say public opinion had changed seriously. He noted that parliamentary elections are due on the 18th or 20th of September and that the war is regarded as a consolidating factor for them.
Put to him that anti-war parties had been blocked from standing, he confirmed that Yabloko had been kicked out of the race.
Fedorov holds no current government office, and his remarks carry no official standing. Figures of his kind are used periodically to place a position in the public domain without the Kremlin owning it, and the construction he uses, attacks carried out not by Russia but by unknown sources, is the same formula applied to the sabotage of undersea cables, arson at warehouses across Europe and parcel bombs placed on cargo aircraft.
British defence manufacturing sites have been treated as a protective security concern for some time. MI5 has warned repeatedly about Russian sabotage plots on British soil, and several prosecutions have followed attacks on premises linked to Ukraine, including an arson at a warehouse in Leyton in east London in 2024 for which men were convicted under the National Security Act.
The interview was broadcast on BBC Newsnight on 24 August.

articles.title: Trump’s Iran ‘economic D-Day’ lands as another threat
articles.body:
For days, U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration had raised expectations of a dramatic announcement, promising an “economic D-Day” against Iran, invoking the term associated with the Allied invasion of Normandy during World War II. In a Truth Social post last Thursday, Trump promised unprecedented economic warfare in an effort to isolate Iran and force it into submission. His Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said the objective was to bring about the regime’s collapse.
Hours before Monday’s news conference, which he had announced several days earlier, Bessent further raised expectations in an opinion article for the Financial Times. “At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary,” he wrote.
But it was not Trump who stepped up to the podium in Washington on Monday. It was Bessent, and the reason soon appeared clear: in practice, the announcement amounted largely to another threat, one of many made since the war began.
Bessent did announce new sanctions targeting around 60 individuals, entities and vessels with links to Iran, but such sanctions announcements are not in themselves unusual. The centerpiece of his announcement was instead a warning to countries around the world: cut all economic ties with Iran or face punishment yourselves.
In prepared remarks before taking reporters’ questions, Bessent said the campaign would intensify gradually until Iran was economically isolated and forced to choose between near-total isolation and compromise in negotiations to end the war. The Treasury Department described the objective as severing Iran’s economic lifelines until Tehran stood alone.
But when Bessent was asked why Washington was not immediately punishing countries that continue to do business with Iran, he effectively acknowledged that doing so could carry severe consequences for the world economy.
The question came from a reporter who noted that the original D-Day was not merely a threat and that the United States had not warned Nazi Germany in advance of the Allied invasion. Why, the reporter asked, were the sanctions not being imposed immediately? “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent replied.
He said Washington wanted to give countries a short period to change course before deploying secondary sanctions, which he described as an extremely powerful tool. Bessent said the administration believed “a warning shot” was appropriate, while making clear that countries that refused to meet U.S. expectations could ultimately find themselves outside the dollar-based financial system.
“We know who they are, they know who they are,” Bessent added, referring to countries that he said continue to provide Iran with a financial or commercial lifeline. He warned that when the “hammer of U.S. Treasury actions” came down on them, they would have only themselves to blame.
But he gave no explicit deadline and did not identify the countries concerned. He also declined to say whether the threat applied to China, which for years has largely ignored U.S. sanctions and continued buying Iranian oil.
China is currently unable to import Iranian crude as it did before because of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. Still, international media noted that the roughly 60 entities targeted in Monday’s sanctions did not include major Chinese financial institutions accused of helping Iran circumvent previous restrictions.
If Trump follows through and imposes sanctions on China, he risks triggering another trade war with Beijing. Analysts believe he would prefer to avoid that for now, particularly with Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to visit Washington next month.
Trump hopes during that visit to extend the temporary agreement reached with Beijing last November, which ended the trade war he had been waging against China. Turkey and Russia also maintain significant economic ties with Iran.
Trump himself made no public reference to the new sanctions campaign on Monday and did not mention it during an event later at the White House. Hours before Bessent’s announcement, however, he posted a brief message on Truth Social about the plunge in Iran’s currency: “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”
In his announcement, Bessent said the United States would focus its new campaign, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” on five sectors that Washington says Iran uses to sustain its economy: digital assets, gold, technology, aviation and shipping.
He indicated that a “major” announcement involving sanctions against a financial institution was expected by the end of the week, although he did not identify it.
During the news conference, however, he specifically mentioned Bank Melli, the Iranian state-owned bank with branches and subsidiaries around the world, including in Britain, France, Germany, Hong Kong and Russia. Bessent said those overseas operations must be shut down or risk exclusion from the U.S. dollar system.
Washington has previously accused Bank Melli of providing financial services to entities involved in Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
Markets were unimpressed too
The relatively muted impact of Monday’s announcement was also reflected in the way it was received by the U.S. media. The New York Times portrayed Bessent’s promised crippling sanctions campaign as having ultimately produced another round of warnings rather than an immediate economic strike.
Financial markets also showed little reaction. Oil prices had risen in the days before the announcement but fell after Bessent spoke, suggesting investors had expected something more consequential.
Market commentary noted that there was little in the announcement that required investors to immediately reassess the economic picture.
Iran, meanwhile, responded dismissively to the announcement. On Monday, Tehran did not repeat the particularly sharp threats of attacks against countries joining what it calls the U.S. “economic war” that had been voiced a day earlier by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
Even before Bessent began speaking, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf dismissed the measure. “The Americans know that no one believes their bluster,” Ghalibaf wrote on X. “The United States is not in an economic position to restrict its relations with other countries any further.”
He said Iran’s trading partners had indicated, both publicly and privately, that they attached little importance to Washington’s statements.
Shortly after the announcement, Iranian Economy and Finance Minister Ali Madanizadeh said the country had prepared in advance for the new measures. He said the latest U.S. sanctions would fail to sever Iran’s economic lifelines just as previous attempts had failed, adding that Tehran had been preparing for such measures for a long time and arguing that the era of a unipolar world had ended.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who on Monday said Iran had tried to assassinate one of his sons, welcomed Bessent’s announcement. In an English-language statement published by his office, Netanyahu congratulated Trump and Bessent on the new sanctions and said they were right to impose a heavy price on the Iranian regime and those enabling its continued aggression.
Trump has shifted strategy in recent weeks after negotiations with Iran reached an impasse and Tehran refused to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the oil artery of the global economy, without U.S. recognition of its control over the strategic waterway. Rather than restart large-scale military action, Trump has opted for an increasingly severe economic blockade.
For now, however, that means global oil prices, and particularly fuel costs for American consumers, are likely to remain high. That in turn is increasing domestic political pressure on Trump to end the war, particularly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Trump has insisted that he is in no hurry despite that pressure, arguing that Americans should understand the economic cost as a price worth paying to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Polls, however, show that the war remains deeply unpopular in the United States and that Trump’s approval ratings have fallen to new lows.
So far, only the United Arab Emirates, once a critical hub for Tehran’s sanctions-evasion networks, has formally announced the suspension of trade with Iran.
But many analysts question whether economic pressure, even if other countries join the effort, can force Tehran into a rapid capitulation. Iran is now operating what has been described as a “survival economy,” designed to minimize the effect of sanctions that it has lived under for decades and repeatedly found ways to circumvent.
In line for dollars in Tehran, spending his last savings: ‘There is no hope’
Still, Iran’s economic crisis has worsened considerably following the two most recent wars. According to the International Monetary Fund, inflation in Iran is expected to approach 70% this year. Since the latest war began, the prices of some foods, including meat, have risen by as much as 150%, while the economy as a whole is expected to contract by a massive 5.4%.
Unemployment has surged, with at least 1 million people losing their jobs since the war began in late February.
Iran’s currency, the rial, had already fallen to a record low of 1.9 million to the U.S. dollar at the beginning of the month and continued to slide ahead of Monday’s announcement. On Sunday it crossed the threshold of 2 million to the dollar, and on Monday it reached 2.02 million. The naval blockade is also depriving Iran of oil-export revenues, with some estimates putting the loss at $435 million a day.
New accounts from inside Iran describe mounting frustration among residents struggling to afford basic food. “We have virtually given up on many things,” Ahmad Karimi, a 52-year-old taxi driver and father of two, told the Associated Press. Karimi works 15-hour days to make ends meet.
“We’re cutting out fruit, we’re cutting out protein, we’ve given up leisure, we even work on weekends,” he said.
Karimi said Iran’s leaders would ultimately have to act to ease the hardship facing him and millions of others. In his view, people cannot continue living under those conditions indefinitely and are increasingly focused simply on getting through each day.
Sadegh Mahmoudi, a 73-year-old Tehran resident, was equally pessimistic about the prospects of an agreement that could bring sanctions relief. “There is no hope for a deal and peace,” he told AP as he waited in line to buy U.S. dollars with what remained of his savings.
Although senior officials in Tehran repeatedly say they recognize the seriousness of the crisis and the hardship facing ordinary Iranians, they insist the Islamic Republic will not surrender.
Ahead of the U.S. sanctions announcement, Iranian officials again threatened escalation, including possible attacks on countries that join the U.S.-led economic blockade.
There have so far been no signs of renewed mass protests against the government, against the backdrop of continued harsh repression and warnings that participation in anti-government demonstrations could be treated as an act of treason punishable by death.
At the beginning of the year, tens of thousands of Iranians were killed by regime forces during nationwide mass protests that erupted amid the economic crisis.
Meanwhile, mediators continue trying to prevent another escalation. Pakistan’s Field Marshal Asim Munir made a brief visit to Tehran on Monday, meeting Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and later President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Munir, who left Tehran within hours, has emerged as a central figure in mediation efforts. A visit he made to Tehran in May helped pave the way for the breakthrough that produced a memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran in June, an agreement that later collapsed.
Qatar’s Al Jazeera reported Monday that Trump had spoken with Munir last week about Iran. Citing a source familiar with the matter, it said Trump asked the Pakistani military chief to use Pakistan’s influence to help restart negotiations.

articles.title: Ukraine allies pledge more air defense support despite Russian threats
articles.body:
Ukraine’s allies pledged on Aug. 24 to increase military support and make air defense an urgent priority, saying Russian threats would not deter them as leaders met in Kiev and by video link on the country’s Independence Day.
The Coalition of the Willing meeting was chaired by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Burnham was in Kiev on his first overseas trip since taking office, alongside several European leaders.
In a joint statement, the coalition condemned Russia’s escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities, infrastructure and civilians. Its members pledged to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses, expand cooperation with its defense industry, share technology and increase sanctions on Russia’s military-industrial sector.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine’s defense,” Burnham said.
He told the meeting that negotiations should begin from the current line of contact and that Ukraine should not be expected to surrender territory Russia had failed to capture on the battlefield.
Macron warned that Moscow was likely to increase provocations against European and NATO countries to deter them from assisting Ukraine.
The European Union separately approved 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) for air and missile defense systems, interceptors, ammunition and radars, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
The funding is part of a 90 billion-euro loan for Ukraine, including 60 billion euros for military needs.
Zelensky said deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles had fallen sharply despite an increase in Russian ballistic attacks. Ukraine received 675 interceptors in 2023 and 364 in 2025, while 264 were projected for 2026, he said.
Kiev is seeking at least another 300 interceptors for the coming winter.
Britain also authorized defense firm MBDA to release classified information on British components used in the SCALP cruise missile, the French version of Britain’s Storm Shadow. The decision will allow France and Ukraine to proceed with plans to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused London of obstructing peace efforts and said Russia would seek to identify and destroy facilities producing the missiles.
Burnham and Zelensky also signed an artificial intelligence partnership giving Britain access to Ukraine’s Avengers battlefield database. The platform uses millions of images gathered by cameras and infrared sensors to train military AI systems.
In return, British universities, researchers and technology companies will provide expertise to support the development of new systems.
The coalition also said it would continue preparations for a multinational force to support Ukraine once a credible ceasefire was in place.

articles.title: Ukraine charges Russian General Staff Chief Gerasimov over deadly July 2 attack on Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukraine charges Russian General Staff Chief Gerasimov over deadly July 2 attack on Kyiv
The Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and the Prosecutor General’s Office reported this, according to Ukrinform.
According to military counterintelligence investigators, since the beginning of the full-scale war, the official has issued combat orders to carry out combined missile and air strikes against civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Investigators established that Gerasimov personally commanded the largest-scale attack on Kyiv overnight on July 2, 2026. Russian forces used a total of 570 weapons against the Ukrainian capital, including attack drones as well as hypersonic and ballistic missiles, including Zircon and Iskander-M missiles.
“More than 100 people were injured in the attack, 70 of whom were hospitalized with injuries of varying severity,” the SSU said.
More than 20 residential buildings in different districts of Kyiv also sustained significant damage.
Based on the evidence collected, SSU investigators served Gerasimov with a notice of suspicion in absentia under Part 2 of Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, concerning war crimes resulting in deaths.
The SSU recalled that, based on evidence gathered by the Ukrainian security service, the International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Gerasimov in June 2024 over war crimes against Ukraine’s civilian population. At the time, the evidence established the Russian general’s direct involvement in missile strikes against Ukraine’s energy system between 2022 and 2023.
As Gerasimov remains in Russia, comprehensive measures are under way to bring him to justice.
As reported, on July 2, Russian forces launched a massive drone and missile attack on Kyiv, with damage recorded in every district of the city. The heaviest destruction was reported at a residential building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district.
Thirty people were killed in the Russian attack overnight on July 2.

articles.title: Iranian Rial Hits Record Low as the U.S. Unveils New Sanctions
articles.body:
Iran’s currency plummeted in value Monday, hitting a record-low open-market rate of 2.02 million rials to the dollar, amid the White House’s launch of “Operation Economic Outcast,” which aims to force concessions from Iran through isolation and a financial stranglehold.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Sunday that an “economic D-Day” was coming, and he shared a first sense of what that might look like at a press conference the following day.
"D-Day marked a historic campaign with our allies,” Bessent said Monday. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
The U.S. announced sanctions on more than 60 targets while expanding sanctionable sectors to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping—which Bessent described as some of the country’s “most vital lifelines.”
The government may also impose secondary sanctions on Iran’s trade partners, Bessent said, adding that those sanctions could roll out in a matter of weeks.
The threat is meant to deter countries from bolstering the country’s waning economy and “collapse every last option for Iran,” Bessent said, describing it as "economic asphyxiation."
Read More: The U.S.-Iran War: By the Numbers
Though Bessent didn’t identify which Iranian partners might be targeted by a new round of sanctions, he did name one financial institution: Bank Melli, the Iranian government-owned bank with branches in about a dozen countries. Bessent said that “every branch” of the bank must be “shuttered and dark” or it will lose access to the U.S. dollar. The Treasury has previously claimed that the bank provides services to entities that support Iran’s nuclear and ballistic programs.
Since the start of its war with Iran on Feb. 28, the Trump Administration has applied both military and economic pressure to achieve its goal of dismantling the nation’s nuclear program.
Bessent’s remarks elaborate on President Donald Trump’s announcement on Aug. 19 that the U.S. would launch “the most crushing economic operation ever mounted” against Iran.
Iran initially dismissed the threat. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday called the U.S. “desperate.” And Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told state television on Aug. 22 that Iran would turn against any neighboring Gulf states that yield to the U.S. in what he called an “economic war.”
“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said.
Given Iran’s sustained control over passage through the Strait of Hormuz, any retaliation could push Brent crude oil above Monday’s closing price of about $92 per barrel or the wartime high of about $120 per barrel.
In a war that has been largely defined by its threat to the global economy, experts wonder whether sanctions against Tehran’s trade allies will further isolate it—and if that will succeed in forcing Iran to capitulate to the demands of the United States.
Could U.S. sanctions force Iran to end the war?
The Trump Administration has argued that in tightening sanctions against Iran, the country will face unprecedented isolation and economic pain.
But Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, tells TIME that the move doesn’t guarantee compliance.
“We really need to keep in mind here that Iran has been under U.S. sanctions for the last 40 years, and we've had several moments in which we have done some sort of a major escalation,” he says. “And each time, it has failed to translate into a policy change from Iran.”
Parsi notes that neither Bessent nor Trump has outlined specific demands for Iran—focusing more on maximum isolation rather than defining clear, achievable diplomatic terms.
Because of this, he argues that Iran is even less likely to succumb to increased pressure.
“What we know of the pattern in the past is that the Iranians will not capitulate—they will escalate,” Parsi says. “This is the same miscalculation Trump made when he thought that the threat of war would cause them to surrender, and instead they prepared themselves for war, and they fought back. And six months later, we're here.”
Further complicating matters is the fact that Iran is meeting with its neighbor, Oman, about regulating passage through the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil formerly passed. Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, is visiting Tehran on Tuesday to continue high-level talks on “bilateral and regional issues.”
Controlling the waterway—a pain point for the global economy—has been Iran’s greatest strength in the war. Any agreement could affect Iran’s leverage over the waterway, although Oman has not publicly endorsed Tehran’s broader demands.
Trump last week threatened that the U.S. would target Oman next if it cooperated with Iran on this matter, telling Fox News: “We’ll bomb the s— out of them.” Experts have said, however, that this is an idle threat and that bombing Oman would be a mistake.
Continuing to enforce its blockade on the Strait does, however, come at a cost to Iran. A June analysis from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies estimated that Iran may be incurring economic damages of about $435 million per day while enforcing it.
How is the plummeting value of the rial affecting Iranians?
Ryan Costello, the policy director at the National Iranian American Council, tells TIME that implementing additional sanctions may not achieve the desired result—but will likely hurt Iranians.
“Regrettably, it has had very harsh impacts on ordinary Iranians—pushing millions out of the middle class, which is often seen as an engine for successful democratic change over time,” Costello says. “This currency depreciation has a real cost for ordinary Iranians, making their life ever more unaffordable.”
According to the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s average annual inflation rate is projected to reach 68.9% in 2026. The depreciation of the rial—which was already the world’s least valuable currency before it dipped this week—will strain Iranian citizens who are already struggling to buy groceries and pay for monthly living expenses.
There is a “real risk” of greater global market destabilization the longer the Strait of Hormuz is closed, Costello says.
“Iran's leadership is signaling that it will respond to intensified economic pressure by further restricting energy flows, and it appears to have the capacity to act on their threat,” Costello says.
In addition to its command of the Strait, he explains: "Iran and other aligned forces are demonstrating an ability to strike energy targets with missiles and drones, both in the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. So Iran and/or its allies could target commercial ships, as well as pipelines, ports, refineries, and other critical energy infrastructure."
And there’s a second major risk if the U.S. places sanctions on certain global powers who buy Iranian oil—particularly economic powerhouse China.
“China could take steps to punish the U.S. economy in turn,” Costello explains.
He says that both risks could be “very damaging,” with economic ramifications that span the globe.
Why Trump is escalating economic pressure on Iran
The U.S.-Iran war is nearing its six-month mark, and peace negotiations have effectively stalled.
The memorandum of understanding established in June—which gave the nations 60 days to work out terms for Iran’s nuclear program and renew uninterrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz—expired Aug. 17. It unraveled in July as the U.S. struck hundreds of targets in Iran, and Tehran retaliated against its allies in the region, including Kuwait and Bahrain. But as the U.S. continued to draw down its munitions stockpiles, Iran held steady with its blockade of the Strait.
Now, Trump has changed his tactics.
“This is where the real problem is: He's going back to economic warfare because military warfare didn't work,” Parsi says.
If additional sanctions fail to force Iran to yield to some of Trump’s demands, Parsi says the President may be running out of options.
“The only exit out of this is actually through diplomacy,” he says. “Otherwise, the U.S. is just going to go back and forth between economic and military action.”
One route to relief may come by way of Pakistan, which helped mediate the June ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran. It dispatched a high-level delegation, led by Field Marshal Asim Munir, to Tehran this week to encourage its leadership to work toward a more lasting peace agreement.
But Parsi contends that the stream of threats from the U.S. may make Iran even less likely to reconcile, saying: “This does not end up becoming the end of the conflict. It just ends up becoming another cycle in the escalation spiral.”

articles.title: Ukraine's UN rep says Russia is losing war against Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukraine's UN rep says Russia is losing war against Ukraine
Andrii Melnyk, Ukraine's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has said that Russia is losing the war it started and that its economy is coming under increasing strain from military spending, sanctions and Ukrainian strikes.
Source: Melnyk speaking at a UN Security Council meeting held on Ukraine's Independence Day, as reported by Ukrinform
Quote: "Irrespective of all the barbaric attacks against civilians in Ukraine, Russia is losing and will lose this war."
Details: Melnyk pointed to the dismissal of Andrei Klepach, chief economist at VEB.RF, Russia's second-largest state-owned bank, reportedly on the Kremlin's direct orders after he made critical remarks about the state of the Russian economy. Klepach had warned, among other things, that Moscow would not be able to win a prolonged economic war against Ukraine.
Melnyk said these remarks represented a rare acknowledgement by a senior Russian economist of the scale of the country's economic problems and directly contradicted Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin's claims that Moscow was successfully overcoming economic pressure.
Melnyk noted that Russia's economy is going through its most difficult period since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is being squeezed by enormous military spending, Western sanctions and Ukraine's growing ability to strike Russia's oil and gas sector.
In the first four months of 2026, Russia's budget deficit reached 5.8 trillion roubles (about US$69.176 billion), significantly exceeding the government's planned deficit of 3.8 trillion roubles (US$45.319 billion) for the whole year.
According to Russia's own Finance Ministry, federal revenues from oil and gas fell by almost 40% year on year in January-April 2026.
Russia is unable to sustain a prolonged war of attrition, as military losses are outpacing recruitment while financial and material costs continue to rise. However, "the Kremlin is exaggerating its tactical advances to prevent and to present the appearance of a continuous military game", Melnyk said.
He also called the UN Security Council's inability to counter Russia's genocidal actions shameful and urged partners to provide Ukraine with all available Patriot missiles.
"What a disgrace that to this day the UN Security Council has failed to take effective action to hold Russia to account and to prevent a daily genocide of the Ukrainian people carried out in plain sight of the world," he said.
Melnyk stressed that Russia had deliberately launched a campaign of ballistic terror against Ukraine, exploiting shortages of interceptor missiles in Ukraine's air defence.
"Knowing that Ukraine is facing critical shortages of air defence interceptors, Putin has unleashed the most cynical and the most brutal campaign of ballistic terror in modern human history, deliberately targeting ordinary people across Ukraine," he said.
Melnyk described the situation as "the most appalling and abhorrent theatre of the absurd imaginable in history", in which Ukraine, a major European state, is "being brutally destroyed before the eyes of the entire international community by Russian ballistic missiles and killer drones".
"And all that the world community seems capable of doing is to convene a meeting of the UN Security Council and at best condemn Russia's war crimes and crimes against humanity being committed on a staggering scale," he said.
Even the strongest words of condemnation of Moscow's criminal actions "cannot stop the killing force of Russian ballistic missiles", he said, calling for decisive action.
This should include imposing "the most painful and far-reaching sanctions" on Russia, particularly against companies producing deadly weapons, in order to force Putin to end the war.
Melnyk also called for an end to Russia's abuse of its veto power, which allows them to evade accountability.
He stressed Ukraine's critical need for Patriot missiles and other advanced air defence systems and urged partners to provide Kyiv with all available interceptors currently in their stocks.
"My fellow citizens find it difficult to understand why missiles capable of saving hundreds of lives every day are being kept in storages instead of being used to shield Ukrainian civilians," Melnyk said.
Previously: During the UN Security Council meeting, Dan Negrea, US Representative to the United Nations Economic and Social Council, called on Russia and Ukraine to stop strikes on civilian targets and return to the negotiating table.
Background: Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said earlier that the UN Security Council would meet on Ukraine's Independence Day to discuss the consequences of Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: What the renewed Black Sea blockade means for Ukraine’s farmers
articles.body:
What the renewed Black Sea blockade means for Ukraine’s farmers
As Ukraine and Russia hammer each other’s Black Sea ports, the amount of grain being shipped through the crucial waterway has slowed to a crawl. For Ukraine’s farmers, the Black Sea blockade could hardly have come at a worse time.
The fields are white for harvest, but the way through the Black Sea is shut.
Faced with a grinding Russian advance towards the last cities in the Donbas left under Kyiv’s control, Ukraine’s state security services in June launched what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called a “40-day campaign” of mid-to-long-range drone strikes deep into Russian territory.
The aim of these strikes, he said, was to put pressure on Moscow by targeting infrastructure vital for the country’s economic life – first and foremost, the oil refineries needed to sustain Russia’s lucrative fossil fuel exports and keep Russian consumers able to fill up at the pump. Kyiv has also carried out deadly air strikes against online retailers’ warehouses that many Russian small businesses rely on to reach their customers.
Read moreLive: Zelensky calls on allies to cover €27 billion gap for Ukraine’s air defence needs
Since July, Ukraine has also targeted Russian ships transporting grain through the Black Sea and hammered rail and port infrastructure around the neighbouring Sea of Azov. Earlier this month, grain terminals at the major port of Novorossiysk – where the remnants of Russia’s Black Sea fleet have taken shelter – came under heavy drone fire from Ukraine.
In response, Russia has stepped up its own strikes on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, raining down drones and missiles on the grain silos and port facilities around the Black Sea city of Odesa and shelling any ship that tries to dock.
For weeks now, Kyiv and Moscow have both struck commercial container ships and grain export terminals in and around each other’s Black Sea ports, effectively cutting off both nations’ ability to ship grain – or anything else – through the crucial sea route.
In a state media interview published Saturday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Ukraine of having “opened … Pandora’s box” and pledged to pummel the embattled nation’s “most sensitive economic sectors”.
Agriculture certainly qualifies. Ukraine’s farmers are among the world’s leading producers of wheat, barley, sunflower seeds and corn, and 90 percent of those exports reach the world through the Black Sea. In peacetime, the country’s thriving agriculture sector made up a full fifth of Ukraine’s economy, and almost half of its exports.
So perhaps it’s no surprise that Zelensky on Sunday said that Russia had rejected Kyiv’s efforts, through third parties, to establish a Black Sea truce that would allow civilian vessels to move through the waters unmolested by either side.
Instead, he alleged, Moscow had insisted that any such deal would only be struck if Kyiv called off its campaign against Russian energy infrastructure, which has triggered worsening fuel shortages across the country. Russia, for its part, has devastated Ukraine’s energy infrastructure throughout the war, trying to starve the country of heat and light as each winter draws near.
Aysmmetric warfare
Oleh Nivievskyi, an associate professor at the Kyiv School of Economics, said that the consequences of the Black Sea blockade weighed far heavier on Ukraine than on Russia.
“For Russia, this is an asymmetric issue, because yes, they export a lot of grain, predominantly wheat,” he said. “But for the economic powerhouse, agriculture is not as important as the energy sector. So on paper it might look the same – Ukraine does not export, and Russia does not export – but it's really asymmetric, because for Ukraine, sea routes are more important economically in terms of the share of exports and in terms of the share of the overall economy.”
Between them, Russia and Ukraine account for more than a quarter of the world’s agricultural exports, most of which feeds people in North Africa and the Middle East. Despite this, Russia’s agricultural exports last year made up less than 10 percent of its total export revenues.
In some ways, we’ve been here before. Tens of millions of metric tonnes of grain remained grounded in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports in the first months of Russia’s February 2022 invasion as Russian ships blockaded the waterway.
Making a deal
As global food prices surged and analysts began to warn of the very real threat of famine in the countries relying upon Black Sea grain, Ukraine, Russia, Turkey and the UN signed the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2022 to carve out a safe passage for ships transporting food and fertiliser through to the Bosphorus Strait.

Moscow pulled out of the deal almost a year to the day later, alleging that Western sanctions continued to interfere with Russia’s own food and fertiliser exports. Despite this, both countries have largely continued to move their agricultural exports through the Black Sea – until now.
Nivievskyi said that the renewed blockade could prove far harsher than that of 2022.
“If you look at this from all angles, the situation is much worse,” he said. “The timing now is to plant winter crops, and winter crops are very important for Ukraine – winter wheat makes up the majority of the wheat that Ukraine produces.”
August is the height of Ukraine’s wheat harvest, and farmers would normally begin harvesting the country’s corn crop next month. If farmers can’t sell this year’s harvests, Nivievskyi said, many will struggle to raise the money they need to plant next year’s crops.
“For this, farmers they would need the liquidity, the working capital, to buy the seeds – and it’s not available right now,” he said. “Usually, around 50 percent of the harvest that’s sold in Ukraine is to purchase the materials for the autumn planting season, and this is now difficult to get because the prices are much lower, and volume-wise we cannot really sell as much as last season. And that’s going to be difficult.”
Storage pressures
With Ukraine’s grain exports down by some 75 percent year-on-year the first two weeks of August, the question of where exactly producers are going to store all the grain they can’t shift is becoming critical. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said the country’s grain storage shortfall could reach as much as 11 million metric tonnes.
All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council deputy chairman Denys Marchuk told DW last week that Ukrainian farmers have already harvested more than 28 million tonnes of grains and pulses – and the corn harvest, estimated at some 33 million metric tonnes, hasn’t even begun.
“The capacities to store the exportable surpluses that Ukraine cannot really export right now are also limited -- and the major harvest is still in the fields,” Nivievskyi said. “So that's also going to create additional pressure on Ukrainian farmers, because they have to store the stuff somewhere.”
As local grain piles up, he added, domestic prices have only fallen further.
“Domestic prices in Ukraine now are quite low compared to the world market prices, and compared to the production costs,” he said. “There are messages and interviews of farmers saying that domestic prices are not at the level of production costs. So they will have to decide whether it’s worthwhile to bring the harvest in – or to keep it in the field.”
And while Russia is trying to reroute its grain shipments through the Caspian and Baltic Seas, Ukraine may struggle to find its own alternatives. The Danube River that has long served as Ukraine’s other major grain route has fallen to historically low levels as droughts wrack Europe, and the ports along its banks come under regular attack from Russian drones and missiles.
Nor can the country’s railways pick up the slack. Ukrainian authorities in July said Russia had damaged more than 200 locomotives in 2026 alone as Moscow systematically targets the country’s rolling stock. According to the agriculture minister, river and rails between them can carry just a third of what used to flow through Ukraine’s Black Sea ports.
Logistics aside, the political landscape has also changed considerably since the opening months of the full-scale war. Where the European Union once liberalised agricultural trade with the beleaguered country, suspending all import duties and quotas to help farmers move their produce west, the resulting influx of Ukrainian wheat and falling prices sparked fierce farmers’ protests across eastern and central Europe. Poland, Slovakia and Hungary all maintain bans on specific Ukrainian agricultural goods in the name of safeguarding their own farmers’ livelihoods.
"The willingness of European partners to help Ukraine out is also not there as it was in 2022," Nivievskyi said.

articles.title: Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
articles.body:
Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
TEHRAN- An open letter signed by a group of Western academics, writers, activists and former and current political prisoners has drawn criticism from other scholars and anti-war activists, who argue that its focus on Iran’s domestic developments risks obscuring the central issue of the conflict: the foreign military assault on the country.
The letter, addressed to what it calls Iran’s “prisoners of conscience,” condemns executions, arbitrary arrests, torture, alleged sham trials and the targeting of ethnic minorities. It describes Iranian political prisoners as being caught “between two blades of a scissors” — one representing the Islamic Republic and the other the United States and Israel.
The signatories call on the Iranian authorities to end executions and release political prisoners, while also calling on Washington and Israel to end what they describe as their “barbaric wars and brutal sanctions.”
The list of signatories includes figures such as Angela Davis, Mumia Abu-Jamal, Judith Butler, Rashid Khalidi, Robin D. G. Kelley, Ruth Wilson Gilmore and Walden Bello, among others.
 
 Yet the letter has prompted a broader debate over whether placing Iran’s political prisoners at the center of the discussion, while the country is under military attack, creates a misleading equivalence between domestic developments and an external war.
Critics question the letter’s political framing
One critic, writing under the name Carlos on X, described the letter as politically problematic despite believing that its signatories included people with long records of opposition to imperialism and political repression.
Noting the participation of figures including Davis, Abu-Jamal, Khalidi, Kelley, Gilmore and Butler, Carlos wrote that these were not people who could simply be dismissed; several had spent their lives in anti-imperialist and Black liberation movements.
But he argued that the letter nevertheless adopted 'a misleading framework.'
Its central metaphor, he wrote, was the image of the Islamic Republic on one side and US-Israeli imperialism on the other, with the Iranian people caught between them. According to Carlos, the framing “inserts a symmetry” between the two sides while failing to adequately distinguish between a state facing an external military attack and the domestic political system governing it.
Carlos also questioned the timing and potential political consequences of the letter. He argued that, regardless of what individual signatories intended, the text could function as part of a broader political narrative used to justify pressure on Iran.
He specifically criticized the letter for invoking allegations including sham trials, systematic torture and the targeting of minorities without providing detailed sourcing in the text. He argued that similar language has historically been used in campaigns preceding regime-change efforts.
His criticism was echoed, in a different form, by Ajamu Baraka, an international human-rights activist and political organizer. Baraka did not reject criticism of Iran itself. Instead, he distinguished between criticizing a government and taking a political position in the context of war.
“No one is above criticism,” Baraka wrote. “Comrades who signed that letter need to understand the difference between criticism & political positioning.”
He argued that the signatories had chosen a political position that, in his view, gave legitimacy to U.S. military violence against Iran.
The reaction from legal scholar Nina Farnia was also critical. Farnia shared material relating to the letter while defending her own position on the conflict. Her broader intervention questioned the decision by progressive voices in the United States and elsewhere to focus publicly on condemning Iran at a moment when, in her view, greater attention should be directed toward opposing the war and sanctions imposed by their own governments.
Historian and scholar Adnan A. Husain similarly questioned the political timing of the letter. In a post responding to the debate, he maintained that publishing an open letter focused on condemning Iran, while the United States and Israel were engaged in military and economic pressure against the country, risked shifting political attention away from opposition to the war.
Husain wrote that the Western left was moving toward public condemnation of Iran “just when” the United States was turning increasingly to economic pressure and political subversion. He argued that activists should instead organize against the war and sanctions imposed by their own government.
David Miller, Political sociologist, producer, and former professor at the University of Bristol said, all signed the disgraceful letter to the Guardian denouncing the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world’s leading anti-imperialist state.
Worse, they compare the Republic with the Zionist/US imperialist aggressor. What we (and they) should be doing is defending the Republic. The Islamic Republic of Iran is not only defending itself, the Palestinians, Lebanon, and the resistance movement. It’s also defending all of humanity and indeed civilization against the depredations of Jewish supremacist imperialism. This is an existential matter for the whole world.
Susan Abulhawa, Palestinian author and activist, has issued a sharp critique of mainstream framing that portrays the US-Israeli confrontation with Iran as a balanced conflict between two equal sides.
In a statement shared on her platform, Abulhawa argues that such framing ignores a "profound asymmetry of power." She describes Iran as a nation crippled by decades of sanctions, now fighting an "existential anti-imperial struggle," while facing a nuclear-armed U.S.-Israeli empire with unlimited military resources, surveillance, and near-total dominance over global political, legal, and information systems.
Abulhawa takes issue with minimizing language in a recent letter, which referred to "current, indiscriminate waves of US-Israeli military assaults." She says that this understates the scale of destruction, citing unprovoked attacks on a school that killed 180 children and teachers, the assassination of Iran's spiritual leader and much of its leadership, and strikes on civilian infrastructure including water systems, farmland, and power grids. She also highlights the downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the U.S., which killed 290 civilians, and decades of assassinations of Iranian scientists and commanders—all of which went unanswered.
The activist also criticizes the letter for failing to contextualize Iranian arrests of detainees, arguing that while some imprisonments may be wrongful, others involve individuals who confessed to espionage for Mossad or terrorism, including a group that brutally murdered a young Quran reciter. She insists that any fair assessment must engage with Iran's legitimate security concerns.
Abulhawa concludes that the conflict is not a symmetrical confrontation but an anti-imperial struggle against overwhelming imperial force distinction, she says, is crucial for honest analysis.
Questions over the signatories’ motives and the letter’s focus
Without direct statements from each signatory, it would be difficult to establish that they all interpreted the letter in precisely the same way.
The criticism therefore raises a legitimate journalistic question rather than providing a definitive answer: what exactly did each signatory intend to endorse?
That question is particularly relevant because the letter was published during a period of military confrontation. The document gives substantial attention to Iran’s domestic political developments, while the external conflict appears largely as one half of a broader framework of “dual oppression.”
For critics, this framing risks placing the government of a country under attack and the states conducting military operations against it within a single conceptual structure, without sufficiently addressing the different forms of power and responsibility involved.
But the timing and framing matter. A government’s policy inside the country and another state’s decision to wage war against that country are separate questions. They can both be condemned, but they carry different legal, political, and moral implications. Treating them as interchangeable risks obscuring the question of responsibility for the conflict itself.
The debate over the letter therefore goes beyond Iran’s domestic politics. It raises a broader question for international intellectual and human-rights circles: how should activists respond when a country facing external military attack is also accused of serious internal repression?
What remains less clear is whether all those whose names appear beneath the letter share the same interpretation of that argument.
That uncertainty is itself significant. The prominence of the signatories may lend the letter considerable political weight, but a list of names cannot, by itself, establish a uniform political position. Determining what each individual intended to endorse would require direct confirmation from the signatories themselves.
Its critics, however, contend that the document’s framing places the aggressor and the state under attack within an overly symmetrical narrative and risks diverting attention from the central question of the war: who initiated the military action, what legal basis was claimed for it, and who bears responsibility for its consequences?

articles.title: AI startups are reshaping the US defense industrial base
articles.body:
- Defense startups like Hadrian and Castelion are using AI-driven manufacturing to compress production timelines once dominated by legacy prime contractors.
- Missile stockpiles fell sharply during the Iran War, driving urgency behind AI-enabled efforts to accelerate rare earth processing and munitions output.
Procurement bottlenecks, rigid legacy contracts and a rare earth supply chain dominated by China have combined to slow the production of missiles and interceptors just as the Iran War has drained U.S. stockpiles to their lowest levels in years. Dr. Guy Kioni, critical minerals initiative fellow at the Cambridge Middle East and North Africa Forum and CEO of the geostrategy consultancy Missang, argues that artificial intelligence, applied from mineral separation through missile assembly, is the tool now compressing decades of slow, incremental progress into a matter of years, and opening the defense sector to a new generation of startups competing with the primes.
Historically, when gas prices go down, consumption goes up. Emissions go up too; people drive more, and the avenues of commerce accelerate. Consumers and entrepreneurs, alike, plan more and do more. Cheaper goods allow people to be more productive. That same relationship holds true for Artificial Intelligence in American industry, which allows more productive firms to grow, hire, expand and scale. In fact, US firms that have invested in integrating AI into their workflows have since expanded their entry-level headcount by 12%, defying expectations that AI would reduce jobs.
No industry shows this better than the Defense sector, where AI is being paired with government contracts that seek accelerated production. The American defense industry has historically been very slow. There are procurement bottlenecks, with long-running chains of bureaucracy that delay and dull innovation. Legacy manufacturers have become inflexible with long-term repetitive contracts and complex supply chains, often structured to appease Congressional constituents. The process has produced a variety of domestic and international chokepoints.
Another chokepoint sits entirely upstream of the factory floor. China refines close to 90% of the world’s rare earths and roughly 94% of the sintered permanent magnets used in missile guidance and radar systems, and it has shown it will restrict export licenses to US defense suppliers with little warning. AI does not change that concentration of power; it shortens how long it takes to build an alternative to it.
AI is doing similar work upstream, separating the critical chokepoint beneath the factory floor. Isolating individual rare earths from complex ore matrices is a chemical engineering challenge requiring dozens of solvent extraction stages, a craft China has refined across four decades. AI is improving the extent to which Western companies can change the calculus.
Aclara Resources and Argonne National Laboratory are now building an AI digital twin to simulate those stages instead of running them by trial and error, accelerate ramp-up timelines and reduce uncertainty at a planned Louisiana separation plant. A comparable AI-controlled rare-earth separation facility in Saskatchewan is now entering commissioning. Neither has replaced Chinese capacity yet. But it’s the same compression driving the factory floor. This is decades of learning curve compressed into years.
The same compression is happening downstream, where the minerals become missiles, and none of it is speculative. AI’s boost to production, jobs, the economy, and defensive readiness is already occurring. Business development within legacy companies like Raytheon and Boeing has been riddled with delays and procurement stagnation; however, at the startup level, entrepreneurship and accelerated manufacturing using AI have begun to reshape how the defense industry functions.
Many new companies stand out. Three-year-old company Castelion, for example, manufactures hypersonic missiles using AI-automated rapid iteration and vertical integration to build out industrial systems constructed for agility and scale. They joined a separate Pentagon agreement to scale production of the Blackbeard hypersonic missile. Manufacturing company Hadrian is another startup that has impressed the defense sector by creating its own AI model, named Opus, for integration into its ‘factory of the future’ for defense production.
Hadrian provides automation tools that can be integrated across factories, for example, reducing lead times for production for Anduril Industries by over 50%. Hadrian, founded in 2020, prioritizes flexibility in the manufacturing process, using Opus to automate production on reduced timescales with sudden changes in procurement needs. The company has hit an $8 billion market cap as it rapidly expands production and its workforce, focusing on building parts for naval defense capabilities.
Zone 5 is another company working to rapidly produce low-cost cruise missiles and interceptors. Caracol AM, similarly, applies Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) and Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) to the defense sector. Both methods are robotic technologies for casting and forging complex and dual-use military components. The company can print parts directly from CAD models using AI, heavily reducing overall lead times.
Under the parallel LCCM program, new agreements and contracts with startups like these will help the Pentagon reach its goal of procuring more than 10,000 low-cost cruise missiles over three years, beginning in 2027. These are just a few examples among many of how AI is used to create real material increases in output.
The ambition is driven by urgency. The Iran War reduced stockpiles of Patriot missiles from 2,200 before the war to fewer than 827. THAAD missiles dropped from 452 to 278. Over 1,000 Tomahawk missiles have been expended since the war began, nearly half of the US’s global inventory. The number is striking considering the US only produced 207 Tomahawk missiles for FY2026. New requests for more will likely not arrive until 2030, after 34 months of production lead time, though a $22.9 billion contract awarded this month aims to ramp annual production past 1,000.
This is why companies that accelerate production are crucial for national security, and it is why AI will show its biggest successes within the defense sector first. Artificial Intelligence has become a tool for increasing productivity by finding efficient new workflows for manufacturing processes, offering substitutive solutions, and accelerating innovation by analyzing and tracking material production. Defense industries have been among the first to showcase these benefits of AI, and increasingly AI has empowered defense startups to receive government contracts in ways never before possible. In the past, they would have been quickly overlooked as incapable or too small, but now AI has advanced the competitive playing field, expanding the number of defense companies and government contracts.
AI is not simply automating the sector. It is one reason startups are now winning contracts once reserved for prime contractors, alongside a deliberate Pentagon shift toward faster, non-traditional procurement. Many economic benefits will stem from the Pentagon’s new strategy. The Defense Department has prioritized contracts that transform industry even amongst legacy companies like Lockheed Martin, which received $53.86 billion for tripling the capacity of PAC-3 MSE interceptors by 2030. They also broke ground on a new facility in Alabama in May of this year, preparing to nearly double production lines for THAAD interceptors. Using AI within the factory will allow Lockheed to produce more at a fraction of the cost while also employing more people to handle the increases in output.
They will undoubtably face heavy competition from startups. That competition, driven in part by the use of AI, should however, result in a more robust, efficient, and productive defense sector, benefiting both national security and the broader American economy.

articles.title: No Tanks, No Troops—Ukraine Sends Its Robot Army Through Kyiv in World-First Drone Parade
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
No Tanks, No Troops—Ukraine Sends Its Robot Army Through Kyiv in World-First Drone Parade
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day with a radically different kind of military display, sending combat robots down Kyiv’s main street, naval drones across the Dnipro River and UAVs into the skies in what Defence Blog described as the world’s first military parade centered entirely on unmanned systems.
The August 24 demonstration replaced the traditional columns of tanks, armored vehicles and marching troops with some of the technologies that have come to define Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Dozens of unmanned ground vehicles rolled along Khreshchatyk in central Kyiv, showcasing robotic platforms designed for combat, reconnaissance, logistics and other frontline missions.
On the Dnipro River, Ukrainian naval drones including the Magura and Sea Baby were displayed. Both families of unmanned vessels have become closely associated with Ukraine’s campaign against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.
The maritime display included reconnaissance platforms, strike drones and versions equipped with air defense missiles, demonstrating how Ukraine has expanded the role of unmanned vessels far beyond their original use as explosive attack craft.
Ukrainian drones also appeared above the capital, including reconnaissance systems, strike UAVs and interceptor drones developed to destroy incoming Russian aerial threats.
The display offered a snapshot of how deeply Ukraine’s military has changed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Drones that initially played mostly supporting roles have evolved into central elements of Ukrainian operations on land, at sea and in the air. Kyiv has since institutionalized that transformation by creating the Unmanned Systems Forces as a dedicated branch of its military.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed legislation establishing the branch in 2024, making Ukraine the first country to build a separate military service specifically around unmanned warfare. June 11 has since been designated as the annual Day of the Unmanned Systems Forces.
The Independence Day demonstration brought many of those technologies together in the center of the Ukrainian capital.
Ukraine had not staged a conventional military parade during the full-scale war. In previous years, Khreshchatyk instead became known for displays of destroyed Russian tanks, armored vehicles and other equipment captured or knocked out during fighting.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.
