articles.title: To further isolate Iran's economy, U.S. rolls out 'D-Day' sanctions
articles.body:
To further isolate Iran’s economy, U.S. rolls out ‘D-Day’ sanctions
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Iranian officials downplayed the significance of the pressure campaign, and suggested it could shut down all oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
- Bessent’s plan to potentially squeeze major economies like China and India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk to the U.S.
WASHINGTON — The United States unveiled plans Monday for new sanctions against Iran that Trump administration officials said are designed to sever Tehran from the global financial system as the nearly six-month conflict between the two countries drags on.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who previewed the announcement last week as “economic D-Day,” described the measures as the opening of an all-out financial assault on the Iranian government and its trade partners — a group that includes China, India, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
“To those who enable Tehran, do not discount the cost of testing Washington’s resolve,” Bessent said at a news conference. “No nation should expect to enjoy the rewards of our system while helping those who seek to destroy it.”
Bessent said it was time for world leaders to “make a decision” between “America and Iran,” adding that President Trump has already been calling foreign leaders to make specific requests ahead of the new sanctions.
But when asked whom the president had been talking to, Bessent said he would not “name names.” He also said the secondary measure would not take effect immediately, arguing that the administration is trying to give “everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior.”
“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent said when a reporter pressed him on why the sanctions weren’t immediate. “We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious.”
After trade negotiations collapsed, President Trump’s 50% tariffs on scores of Canadian imports kicked in over the weekend. A look at what that means.
The pressure campaign will build on a naval blockade and other sanctions the Trump administration has already imposed in its effort to force Tehran into a deal that ends the war on U.S. terms.
Trump’s latest economic push against Iran revives a familiar strategy from presidents of both parties, using financial leverage to pressure Tehran toward more serious negotiations over its nuclear program. Sanctions helped bring Iran to the table before a 2015 nuclear deal brokered by President Obama, but the agreement was widely criticized as weak by Republicans. After Trump withdrew from the agreement in his first term, a new “maximum pressure” campaign failed to secure a new deal.
Trump’s decision to return to a strategy of economic coercion has signaled to Iran that the fighting phase of the war is probably over, for now, with the U.S. administration choosing a path “neither of war nor of peace,” Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, said this week.
Iranian officials, who had been anticipating the move, pushed back on Washington’s strategy even before Bessent began speaking Monday.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian state media over the weekend that the sanctions amounted to a repackaged version of decades-old American pressure tactics that Tehran has already learned to withstand. Esmail Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, warned of “grave consequences” for any countries cooperating with what he said was “illegal behavior” by the United States. And Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme Security Council, suggested that the economic pressure could shut down oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, a threat that would ripple through global energy markets.
That defiance underscores the central gamble of Washington’s strategy. Rather than aiming sanctions at Iran alone, Bessent’s plan to potentially squeeze major economies like China and India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk to the U.S.
The fallout could also reach beyond foreign diplomacy as a hit to global markets also risks compounding Trump’s troubles at home ahead of the midterm elections, as Americans grow unhappy with the economy and their support for the conflict in the Middle East plummets. The Iran sanctions also land as the administration wages a separate trade fight with Canada, adding uncertainty to global and domestic markets.
Whether Washington will be able to apply pressure on Iran’s trade partners remains an open question.
China alone shares nearly $10 billion in bilateral trade with Iran, and paid roughly $31.2 billion for unreported Iranian crude oil imports in 2025, according to the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. That makes China the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil by a wide margin, accounting for more than 90% of Iran’s oil exports, according to the commission.
It is unclear whether Trump has spoken to China’s leader, Xi Jinping, about the sanctions. But the two leaders are set to meet in Washington next month, adding to the diplomatic dynamics of the moment.
Other trading partners have already made some moves.
The UAE said last week that it was suspending trade with Iran, a decision that followed accusations that Tehran had fired two ballistic missiles at the Emirates.
Afra Al Hameli, a spokesperson for the Emirati Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a post on Aug. 18 on X that all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice. She added that the Emirates was “firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system.”
Bessent said Monday that he expects other countries will “take similar actions as we continue our engagement.”
In an opinion article written for the Financial Times last week, Bessent has cast the new measures as the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary.”
Bessent wrote that countries that “sever Iran’s remaining financial and commercial connectivity” will see their economies reinvigorated, and those who don’t will experience the end of their “lasting prosperity.”
President Trump is betting ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can finally force Tehran to accept a peace deal on U.S. terms. But, as with similar efforts before, Iran may be impervious to such pressure.
“Any nation that serves as a financial artery of a withering regime should expect to share in its isolation,” he wrote. “To become a sanctuary for terror is to become, in the eyes of the United States, a global pariah.”
Ahead of the announcement Monday, Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran was “completely collapsing.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said the U.S. had already done all that it can against Iran and that the central bank had been shoring up its foreign currency reserves for months. Last week, he said Iran’s crude exports had “virtually stopped.”
“[The Americans] have done everything, so what else can they do?” he said in an interview with Tasnim News.
Despite his assurances that the central bank was working on preventing a devaluation of the Iranian rial, the currency has struggled to remain above a black market exchange rate of 2 million per dollar — a record low. The Central Bank rate stands at roughly 1.5 million rial to the dollar.
Though experts question the effectiveness of additional economic pressure on Tehran, Bessent’s threat to target Iran’s trading partners — especially the UAE, China and Turkey, who together comprise almost three-quarters of Iran’s foreign imports — will undoubtedly be painful for Iranians.
For example, Iran uses the UAE as a reexport hub and buffer, and receives vehicle spare parts from China, according to the Observatory for Economic Complexity. Iranian economic experts say both the agricultural and pharmaceutical sectors also rely on imports from countries such as Brazil and Turkey.
Ceballos reported from Washington and Bulos from Beirut.

articles.title: Air Force ‘Closely Following’ Navy’s New Long-Range Air-to-Air ‘Malice’ Missile
articles.body:
A new Navy missile could fill a long-range air-to-air need for the U.S. Air Force’s fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-generation fighters.
The Navy’s portfolio acquisition executive for munitions posted information on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile online on Aug. 22, the same day it unveiled the project at the service’s annual Tailhook Symposium in Reno, Nev.
The Raytheon missile is geared for Marine and Naval aviators’ fighter platforms, from the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, with a range “in excess of 250 nautical miles.”
“Also known as Malice, the LRAAM directly supports the Department’s contribution to integrated deterrence by increasing range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for Marine and Naval Aviation forces that are defending our fleets, our interests, and our homeland,” according to a Navy statement emailed to media. “Further details regarding specific capabilities and deployment timelines remain classified to protect operational security.”
Malice’s advertised range is well more than that of the Lockheed Martin AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, said to be beyond 120 miles, and the Raytheon AIM-120D Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, around 100 nautical miles. The Air Force is taking the lead in developing JATM for itself and the Navy.
“With increased range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for naval forces, the AIM-424 delivers a generational leap in long range air-to-air combat capability that can out range any threat,” Phil Jasper, president of Raytheon, said in an email statement.
Malice Data
- Contractor: Raytheon
- Propulsion: Solid-propellant rocket motor
- Length: 13.5 feet
- Diameter: 13.5 inches
- Wingspan: 26.2 inches
- Weight: 1,500 pounds
- Range: In excess of 250 nm
- Warhead: Blast fragmentation
Source: Navy
But while Malice represents a major increase in range over current missile programs, it falls short more ambitious efforts early in development like the Air Force Long Range Weapon, which seeks distances of more than 1,000 nautical miles. The Air Force first revealed plans for the AFLRW in June.
“The Air Force is closely following the progress of the Navy on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile Program,” an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine on Aug. 24. The spokesperson declined to answer additional questions.
The two services often partner on missiles for their aircraft, such as JATM, AMRAAM, and the AIM-9X Sidewinder.
“The Navy and Air Force have different operational requirements, but in areas such as fighter-launched offensive weapons, each can benefit from the other’s technological advances, testing, and development,” said retired Air Force Col. John “JV” Venable, senior resident fellow at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “Malice appears to be another example of how parallel efforts can accelerate capability and produce benefits across the Joint Force.”
The Navy has also developed the AIM-174B Gunslinger, which has a range of 150-200 nautical miles, but that missile won’t fit in the internal weapon bays of the F-35 and F-22, limiting its usefulness to the Air Force.
The new Malice missile, on the other hand, is meant to go a wide range of aircraft, including sixth-gen fighters like the Navy’s not-yet-named F/A-XX and the Air Force’s parallel project, the Boeing F-47.
“The long-range missile fight is much like a jousting contest: the fighter with the longer lance has a major advantage,” said Venable, a former F-16 pilot and commander. “Chinese beyond-visual-range missiles are assessed to outrange many current U.S. weapons, potentially giving Chinese fighters the opportunity to shoot first by dozens of miles.”
The Malice missile would “extend U.S. engagement range, improve first-shot opportunities, and help restore our tactical advantage against peer adversaries,” he said.
Beyond the tactical level, Venable noted, having a missile like Malice in the fighter community’s quiver would give commanders greater flexibility in operational planning and offset numerical disparity with a potential peer fight.
“The People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) already holds a significant advantage in the numbers of fighters it can generate over Taiwan compared with the U.S. and allied forces,” he said. “We need every technological advantage available to offset that numerical disparity.
Roots
Aviation Week reported that Malice has a two-stage design—reminiscent of a decade-old program known as the Long Range Engagement Weapon, developed in the mid-2010s under then-Secretary of Defense Ash Carter.
Flight Global reported at the time the LREW effort was also a two-stage design that would eventually transition to multiple services. The Air Force was known to be working on the weapon while also developing the JATM – both efforts sought to replace the decades-old AMRAAM, which debuted in the mid-1980s.
The JATM is seen as a direct replacement for fighters to carry instead of the AMRAAM. But the LREW’s two-stage design promised a far greater range.

articles.title: Ukraine must be competitive with Russia in number of deep strikes – Zelensky
articles.body:
Ukraine must be competitive with Russia in number of deep strikes – Zelensky
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this at a press conference following the Coalition of the Willing summit in Kyiv, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Regarding deep strikes, we have sufficient capabilities to increase production. If we increase production, we will be able to carry out more attacks and respond,” Zelensky said.
He noted that Ukraine already has various types of drones with a strike range of 350 to 3,000 kilometers, including drone missiles, with which successful operations have already been conducted.
“But we do not have sufficient funding for this,” Zelensky said, while thanking the EU for providing the €90 billion loan, with €60 billion earmarked for defense assistance.
The president noted that Russia is increasing the number of its own long-range strikes.
“Two years ago, there were 40 Iranian Shaheds, then 100, when we didn’t know what to do, but we found a way, then 300, and today there are 500 or 1,000 during massive attacks,” Zelensky said.
He added that in order to put pressure on Putin, Ukraine needs a comparable number. “Not in terms of money, because they currently have twice as much money as we do. Even more. It is about €340 billion, whereas in 2027 we will spend €140 billion. So we need to be competitive in the number of long-range strikes,” the president said.
He explained that he was referring not to ballistic missiles but to other strike capabilities.
“We need more money. Much more,” he concluded.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Finnish President Alexander Stubb believes that strikes on oil refineries and logistics warehouses in Russia increase the share of Russians who want the war to end and are therefore part of Ukraine’s smart military strategy.

articles.title: Shortage of engineers becomes a bottleneck for Ukraine’s defence tech
articles.body:
Shortage of engineers becomes a bottleneck for Ukraine’s defence tech
- Ukraine's defence tech industry faces a severe engineer shortage, limiting the ability to quickly respond to frontline innovation needs.
- The labour gap is worsened by population decline, war impacts, and a lack of qualified candidates despite rapid workforce growth.
- Companies train inexperienced workers and boost salaries, but specialised skills remain scarce, threatening long-term defence innovation and production scaling.
AI generated
KYIV – The speed of innovation on the Ukrainian battlefield means frontline troops may need a new drone design within weeks – but the country’s defence industry faces a critical labour shortage that threatens to derail that pace.
Tens of billions of dollars in investments and wartime demand have fuelled the creation of thousands of defence companies in Ukraine, but the supply of workers has failed to keep up.
Yurii Faraponov, chief operating officer of BlueBird Tech, said his company can’t respond to some frontline requests because he doesn’t have enough engineers.
Another company recently poached a production manager by offering him three times his previous salary, along with paid housing, said Sergii Vysotskyi, vice-president of the National Association of Ukrainian Defence Industries.
Some companies are tracking down retired specialists and begging them to return to work.
The labour shortage is emerging as one of the biggest bottlenecks to expanding Ukrainian weapons production and accelerating innovation, industry insiders say.
“The market is experiencing something akin to internal cannibalism: we keep reaching out to the same people over and over and using every tool” to recruit them, said Marta Khrypiak, defence tech lead at the Lobby X recruitment agency.
Ukraine’s working-age population had been shrinking for decades and fell even more sharply after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, as millions fled abroad and others joined the military.
In defence tech, the shortage cuts directly into Ukraine’s bet that technology will offset its manpower disadvantage on the battlefield.
An April survey of 27 defence tech companies by the CORE Team recruitment agency found that the firms had grown their workforce by more than 50 per cent – collectively hiring thousands of people – in one year.
All expected to expand further, but said there was a lack of qualified candidates.
Even before the war, technical and vocational education had became less popular and many specialists left for better-paid work abroad, Vysotskyi said.
The number of professionals is rising as people retrain, said CORE Team Chief Executive Officer Anna Korol, but the industry is growing much faster.
Some specialities – hardware developers, radio-frequency and antenna specialists, chemists needed for explosives manufacturing – are so scarce that recruiters say they effectively know all available candidates.
“You can’t recruit many people through job postings anymore – everyone has already been snapped up,” Vysotskyi said.
The lack of people is particularly damaging to innovation, several industry representatives said, as weapons become more sophisticated and require more specialised expertise.
Scaling suffers as well.
Even when a company can find enough welders and assemblers, for instance, there are too few production managers and process engineers to oversee and expand manufacturing lines, Vysotskyi said.
When a company needs to deliver on a tight deadline, job titles can become irrelevant: accountants and human resources workers may be pulled in to help assemble drones or load shipments, Khrypiak said.
There is no work-life balance, she added, with long hours at production sites targeted by Russian strikes.
That leads to fewer applicants: defence tech vacancies drew just an average of 1.5 to 3.8 applications in July on DOU.ua, a popular tech job board, compared with dozens for civilian software roles.
But workers in the industry care that their ultimate customer is a soldier, Faraponov said.
“When you compare your pace of work with the pace of the military, you don’t really feel like complaining,” he added.
The sense of purpose often drives people to the industry, according to recruiters, but there are tangible perks too.
Almost nine in 10 companies had raised salaries over the previous year, according to the CORE Team survey, to stay competitive.
Companies are aggressively headhunting specialists at home and trying to return others from overseas, industry insiders say.
People with rare expertise sometimes work for multiple manufacturers at once.
Military-aged men at defence companies also get an exemption from the draft.
And career growth opportunities are unparalleled for Ukraine, recruiters say.
Faraponov, for instance, worked in marketing before joining BlueBird Tech in 2024 to assemble drones in a garage-like workshop.
Within two years, as the company expanded, Faraponov led production at a factory and then became the company’s chief operating officer.
Such advancement is not uncommon.
Raising a new generation of engineers
Companies, unable to find experienced employees, increasingly take people with no tech background, then train them.
Assembly workers can be trained in weeks, said Maryna Shvydchenko, human resources director at Vyriy Drone.
The company runs an academy to prepare people with no relevant experience for production jobs, then grows many of them into managers and team leaders.
Training research and development employees takes longer, which puts a premium on university-educated specialists.
Since 2022, Ukrainian universities have been offering or reviving defence-related degree programmes.
All 32 first graduates of one such programme – master’s in unmanned aerial vehicles at the Kyiv School of Economics – were immediately snapped up by the UAV industry, according to Ivan Ostroumov, the programme’s head.
Although defence-tech-adjacent majors saw an uptick in enrolment across universities since the full-scale invasion in 2022, the gains have not kept pace with the industry’s growing demand.
In 2025, according to government data, only 671 students nationwide started bachelor’s degrees in aerospace engineering, which encompasses drone and missile manufacturing, and 464 chose chemical engineering, badly needed for explosives manufacturing.
“Obviously, it’s never too late because Russia will not disappear from the agenda as our enemy,” Vysotskyi said.
“As long as that existential threat exists, we will always need a very strong, technologically advanced defence industry, which requires a skilled workforce.” BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Ozon next in Kyiv’s sights as sheds of Wildberries rival burn
articles.body:
- 
  Ukraine has targeted four more warehouses of Ozon – Russia’s second-largest online retailer after Wildberries, which has itself been crippled by Ukrainian attacks. Ozon’s shares fell by almost 30% on Monday after it reported strikes in southern Russia that brought to six the number of its facilities targeted within three days. Ozon said a logistics hub in Makhachkala in Dagestan was on fire and had halted operations after a drone attack in which “several people” were injured. Another was on fire in Enem on the outskirts of the city of Krasnodar, while workers were evacuated from warehouses that came under attack in Adygeysk, in the Adygeya region, and in Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.
- 
  In earlier events, drone strikes halted work at an Ozon logistics centre in the Samara region and another in the Orenburg region. Financial analysts said that unlike privately owned Wildberries, which has the backing of state-owned bank VTB, Ozon’s main shareholder AFK Sistema has a large debt and is unlikely to provide substantial support. Before the latest Ozon attacks, Vladimir Putin promised state help in the restoration of warehouses “at a new technological level” and asked the government to design a programme to help the sector. The EU imposed sanctions on Ozon’s and Wildberries’ financial units on 24 July.
- 
  Putin has geared up the Russian state to seize control of companies like Wildberries and Ozon, as well as fuel companies and transport operators, by deeming them too poorly protected from Ukrainian attacks. Special powers set out in a presidential decree will allow the state to take charge of them at a time when Ukraine has stepped up drone attacks on oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses. The state will be able to seize physical and financial assets, and assume formal ownership rights, if entities responsible for such facilities are judged to have failed to protect them and are too slow to repair them after any attack. It applies to fuel, energy, industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities and other objects regarded as critically important for security and economic stability.
- 
  The Ukrainian military struck a Russian Mig-29 fighter plane and two Russian vessels in the Black Sea, Ukraine’s drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said on Monday. It is the third Russian warplane hit in two days. Brovdi said on the Telegram app that one of the vessels attacked was a tanker and the other was a bulk carrier. Ukraine’s military struck a Russian military plant at Kamensky in the Rostov region, causing a fire, the Ukrainian general staff said. The plant produces solid rocket fuel for Russian weapons.
- 
  The Perm oil refinery, Russia’s seventh-largest by volume, has shut down after a Ukrainian drone attack on 21 August, two industry sources told Reuters. The primary CDU-4 unit, which accounts for almost 40% of the plant’s capacity, stopped working on that day. Repair works could take between one and two weeks. Another primary refining unit, CDU-5, which accounts for 34% of the plant’s capacity, has been idle since a 29 July drone attack. Lukoil, which controls the refinery, did not reply to a request for comment. The plant usually makes millions of tonnes of petrol and diesel.
- 
  Andy Burnham urged Ukraine’s allies to “dig into our own stocks” to provide it with more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying it “needs more help to protect its people right now”. The British prime minister chaired his first meeting of the “coalition of the willing” in Kyiv as Ukraine celebrated its independence day. Burnham said the coalition was “doing everything we can all do and working with our allies outside of this coalition to dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”. He called on the US Congress to “ratchet up” economic pressure on Russia as it struggles with a record budget deficit and declining oil revenues.
- 
  Ten Ukrainian prisoners of war who were thought to be missing in action have been released in a prisoner exchange, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He did not mention Russia in his statement, saying only that the prisoners had been released via Belarus, one of Moscow’s closest allies. Russia did not immediately say if Kyiv had returned soldiers in the exchange.

articles.title: Air defence, sanctions and multinational forces: what Coalition of the Willing agreed on in Kyiv
articles.body:
Air defence, sanctions and multinational forces: what Coalition of the Willing agreed on in Kyiv
Leaders of the Coalition of the Willing have said after their meeting in Kyiv that they have agreed to step up military support for Ukraine, boost its air defence capabilities, impose further sanctions on Russia and prepare multinational forces.
Source: a joint statement by the leaders of the Coalition of the Willing posted on the UK government website, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The statement says the leaders condemn Russia's systematic and intensifying attacks on Ukrainian cities, critical infrastructure, civilian facilities and cultural heritage sites, which have recently caused the highest civilian casualties since the beginning of the full-scale war.
The leaders stressed that Ukraine has an unequivocal right to defend itself in the war of aggression launched against it by Russia and that threats from Moscow will not deter them from supporting Ukraine.
"They expressed their determination to increase military support to Ukraine, strengthen its air defence as a matter of urgent priority, enhance cooperation with its defence industry, and share relevant technologies, including through the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition," the statement said.
They also agreed to step up sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex and those supporting its operations, to provide immediate energy support for Ukraine to prepare for the coming winter. They stressed the need to support Ukraine's economic resilience amid Russia's attempts to block exports through Black Sea ports.
The leaders agreed to continue efforts to restrict Russia's financial resources for waging the war through sanctions and measures to combat sanctions circumvention, including action against Russia's shadow fleet.
According to their estimates, joint measures in this area have prevented Russia from earning around US$495 billion throughout the full-scale war.
They welcomed the US Senate's decision on steps to increase economic pressure on Russia and committed to working closely with the United States in the near future on coordinated measures.
Quote: "The leaders commended President Zelenskyy's continued readiness to enter into meaningful peace talks, in order to bring about a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, and reiterated their call for Russia to agree to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire starting from the line of contact.
The Coalition would continue to prepare the Multinational-Force Ukraine to deploy once a credible cessation of hostilities was in place, as part of a wider set of robust politically and legally binding security guarantees to ensure Ukraine's future security and prosperity once a ceasefire enters into force."
Background:
- Following the Coalition of the Willing meeting, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Kyiv's international partners have pledged support for Ukraine through "military and energy aid packages".
- He is asking for the next meeting in this format to be held this autumn.

articles.title: General Atomics Plans ‘Wildfire’ Drone for Pentagon’s Low-Cost MMA Program
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems predicts the new drone it plans to pitch for the military’s “Massed Modular Aircraft” program will exceed many of the military’s requirements for a successor to the MQ-9 Reaper.
Wildfire, as General Atomics has dubbed it, “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” company spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement, though he declined to specify the drone’s expected capabilities or cost. Aviation Week first reported the company’s plans for Wildfire.
MMA is intended to be a low-cost, attritable drone that could fly in groups if needed and take on some missions now performed by the MQ-9 Reaper, which was also made by General Atomics. The Defense Innovation Unit released a solicitation July 7 asking companies to submit ideas for the new drone concept, which is meant “to execute missions that the MQ-9A performs today.”
The Air Force is partnering with DIU on the MMA effort, which it said “will directly inform the requirements for the MQ-9’s successor.”
DIU’s solicitation called for drones to be able to carry a payload of at least 2,800 pounds—roughly the weight of one Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile, or LRASM—and have an unrefueled combat radius of at least 2,300 nautical miles, while carrying a payload, as well as being able to fly a one-way ferrying flight of at least 8,000 nautical miles.
The Pentagon wants MMA drones to be able to launch weapons, collect intelligence, conduct electronic warfare, or relay communications while staying airborne for long periods. DIU said that is intended to exhaust an enemy and force them to burn through pricey anti-aircraft missiles and other resources.
While General Atomics did not detail what Wildfire—a medium-altitude long endurance drone—will be able to do, Brinkley’s statement hinted at some of the goals the company set out to achieve.
“How do we come out of the box, day one, with a 10,000 nautical mile ferry range?” Brinkley said. “Can we carry four LRASMs? Can we swarm 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control? Can we fuse all of that data into a highly effective common operating picture? Can we do that at scalable, affordable mass?”
The Air Force has lost dozens of MQ-9 drones since operations against Iran launched in late February. The Washington Post reported earlier in August that about 45 Reapers have been lost, in some cases shot down, during Operation Epic Fury.
In its original solicitation, DIU said that with adversaries increasingly using low-cost antiaircraft capabilities to create layered defenses, the military won’t be able to rely on “exquisite” aircraft with price tags north of $30 million. For that reason, DIU and the Air Force said, the military needs drone capabilities that can weather some losses while still being able to accomplish their missions.
The Air Force and DIU want these new drones to be modular so they can be quickly updated with payloads like full-motion video sensors, so an MMA could carry out some of the MQ-9’s current missions. An Air Force official told reporters earlier in August that the service wants to start awarding contracts by the end of this year.
DIU also wants contractors to be able to flight test a full-scale prototype 21 months after receiving the award and to be able to deliver 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031.
Brinkley said General Atomics “can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”
However, Brinkley said, the military has an “immediate, critical ISR gap” that Wildfire would not be able to fill in the short term. General Atomics has options that could serve as an interim bridge, he said, and the company is now discussing those with Pentagon decision-makers.
General Atomics did not reveal any imagery or concept art for Wildfire.

articles.title: Burnham plans trip to New York as Ukraine pleads for US-made missiles
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has said he is likely to go to the UN general assembly gathering in New York next month, a potential chance for the new prime minister to meet a host of world leaders.
While Downing Street say the plans are not definite, the prime minister told Bloomberg in an interview: “I’m looking forward to going to New York in September.”
Speaking in Kyiv after a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Burnham went on: “I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion. Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
If it did take place, it would be Burnham’s first visit to the US since taking office, and could also potentially provide an opportunity for a first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump.
Dozens of world leaders gather annually for the general assembly. This year’s high-level meeting takes place from 22 to 28 September, which could be logistically tricky for Burnham given Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool begins on 27 September.
But attending would give Burnham the opportunity to meet a number of other world leaders in one go, even if bilateral talks tend to be brief amid the frenetic schedule of the gathering.
Burnham’s policy background is predominantly domestic, and since entering No 10 he has had to rapidly develop a foreign policy – thus far very similar to that of Keir Starmer – and get to know world leaders.
In Kyiv on Monday, for his first official overseas trip since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham laid a wreath for Ukraine’s independence day, joining a series of other European leaders, including the European council president, António Costa.
He also used the trip to announce that the UK government would allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version.
During his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said there would be “no change in the UK’s steadfast support” for Kyiv.
He also urged Ukraine’s allies to send more Patriot missiles to Kyiv as Ukraine struggles under continued Russian bombardment, and co-chaired his first coalition of the willing meeting, where he said the group was doing “everything we can” to “dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly pleaded for more the US-made interceptor missiles in recent months as Kyiv’s stocks have diminished. Supplies of Patriots have been diverted to the Middle East since the outbreak of the US’s war with Iran, with Ukraine receiving significantly fewer missiles this year than in previous years.
During the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt “really confident” the problem was “fixable”, but added: “There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with. It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation.”
Russia has sought to capitalise on the shortage by stepping up its ballistic missile strikes, killing at least 23 people and wounding more than 100 in the past three days.
Russia has threatened unspecified potential retaliation against the UK for what Moscow says is increased involvement in the conflict.

articles.title: Philippines seeking to expand military drone capabilities in modernization push, defense chief says
articles.body:
The Philippines plans to expand its unmanned capabilities, including through the development and acquisition of drones as part of efforts to modernize its military, its defense chief said on Tuesday.
US defense ally the Philippines also plans to acquire additional guided-missile corvettes and other major defense assets to beef up its external defense capabilities, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro told a budget hearing in the lower house of Congress.
The Philippines has shifted its security focus from internal threats to external security as tensions rise with Beijing in the South China Sea, where confrontations between them over disputed features inside Manila's exclusive economic zone have grown in frequency in recent years.
The armed forces currently operate a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles that provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Teodoro said.
"As we mature on the cycle, then we can acquire more," Teodoro said in pitching to lawmakers a 6.3% increase in the defense ministry’s budget for 2027, from the 305.5 billion pesos ($4.95 billion) spending plan approved for this year.
Drone expansion is part of a proposed 50 billion pesos ($810.4 million) allocation for the Philippines' modernization program next year, 25% higher than that of the current budget.
Philippines seeking integration for drones
The priority was also developing the systems, connectivity, and operational know-how needed to use drones effectively, Teodoro added.
"More than the personnel, it is the integration into the operation, what do you do with them and how do you use them," he said. Developing secure communications and network capabilities was crucial, he added.
Teodoro declined to identify specific systems under consideration, saying the details were classified and highly sensitive.
"They are very, very sensitive to compromise, particularly with AI," he said, adding that the Philippines was in close contact with several countries with expertise in drone technology.
Yuliia Fediv, Ukraine’s ambassador to the Philippines, told Reuters in June that Kyiv has been in discussions with Manila over drone technology cooperation.
In June, the United States said it has given the Philippine military four solar-powered sea drones to boost its maritime surveillance.

articles.title: Ukraine, UK sign landmark AI deal
articles.body:
Ukraine, UK sign landmark AI deal
Ukrinform reports this with reference to the UK government.
The AI partnership agreement, signed in Kyiv by President Volodymyr Zelensky and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, will give Ukraine access to support from world-leading universities, researchers and technology companies, as well as the world's third-largest AI ecosystem.
The UK is set to become the first international partner to gain access to Ukraine's Avengers AI Labs, enabling the two countries to accelerate the development of AI tools designed to shape the battlefield.
“By combining Ukrainian battlefield data with British expertise, we will accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home,” the UK government said.
The platform provides real world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine.
These sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, including tanks, artillery, air defense systems, infantry and aerial targets such as Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, feeding the data into Avengers AI Labs to train new AI models.
Under the partnership, the UK and Ukraine will also explore other platforms for cooperation.
The UK government described Avengers AI Labs as “a goldmine of battlefield data” that will give British innovators and researchers unprecedented access to real operational data and the ability to rapidly develop and test new technologies.
In turn, the UK will provide Ukraine with access to world-leading universities, researchers, technology companies and its extensive AI ecosystem, enabling Ukraine to draw on British expertise to accelerate the development of solutions to urgent challenges and turn hard-won battlefield experience and unique datasets into technologies that will benefit both countries.
“This groundbreaking partnership will bring together Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience with Britain’s world-class AI ecosystem, giving us the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine,” Prime Minister Burnham said.
“Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading innovators in defence technology, forged through courage, ingenuity and the hard lessons of war,” he added.
As reported, during his first foreign trip as Prime Minister, Burnham assured Ukraine that he would work to strengthen assistance to the country, particularly in air defense and countering Russian missile strikes.
Earlier, the UK government announced that it would allow European defense company MBDA to declassify information on British components used in Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles for Ukraine.

Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time

Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
Ukrainian drones reached Russia’s northern Arkhangelsk region, home to the strategic Plesetsk military cosmodrome used to launch military satellites and intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to OSINT analysis published by Russian independent media outlet Astra on August 23.
The incident appears to mark the first documented case of Ukrainian drones reaching the Arkhangelsk region, extending Kyiv’s deep-strike reach into Russia’s far north.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian monitoring resource Locator Rossii reported that at least two drones reached the Plesetsk area.
ASTRA analyzed photographs taken by local residents and said smoke could be seen rising in the vicinity of the military spaceport. The images were reportedly taken from Mirny, a closed city established during the Soviet era specifically to support operations at Plesetsk.
The exact target and consequences of the reported drone operation remain unclear.
Astra also geolocated footage published by Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ showing a drone flying above Kargopol in the Arkhangelsk region. The aircraft was traveling in the direction of Plesetsk, located roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, away.
Local residents separately recorded two drones flying through the region and posted footage of the aircraft online.
Temporary flight restrictions were introduced at an airfield near the Plesetsk Cosmodrome because of the potential drone threat, under Russia’s emergency airspace closure procedure known as the Carpet Plan.
Plesetsk is Russia’s principal northern military spaceport and plays a significant role in both its military space program and strategic missile testing.
Russia has repeatedly launched Soyuz-2 and Angara rockets carrying military spacecraft from the facility. The cosmodrome is also being used to deploy Rassvet communications satellites, part of Moscow’s effort to build a domestic satellite internet network comparable to SpaceX’s Starlink.
Russia plans to have 292 Rassvet communications satellites in orbit by the end of 2027, making the program increasingly important for Moscow’s communications infrastructure.
Plesetsk also serves a separate strategic military role as a launch site for Russian intercontinental ballistic missiles.
No confirmed information has yet emerged regarding damage at the cosmodrome or whether Plesetsk was the drones’ intended target.
Russia continues to deploy its “Rassvet” satellite constellation, which is intended to serve as an analogue to Starlink.
However, the project requires regular launches of carrier rockets. The first two groups of Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit using Soyuz-2.1b rockets manufactured by the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara.
Production of carrier rockets is one of the key constraints on the deployment of the constellation. The satellites can also be launched from the Plesetsk and Vostochny spaceports in Russia, as well as the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: UK PM plans to persuade Trump to help Ukraine with Patriot missiles – Bloomberg
articles.body:
UK PM plans to persuade Trump to help Ukraine with Patriot missiles – Bloomberg
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he and other European leaders plan to visit the United States next month to persuade President Donald Trump to give Ukraine access to some of the US stockpiles of Patriot interceptor missiles ahead of winter.
Source: Burnham in a comment to Bloomberg
Quote: "I'm looking forward to going to New York in September."
Details: Bloomberg noted that Burnham was referring to the upcoming UN General Assembly session in New York. It will be his first visit in his capacity as prime minister.
Quote: "I've not fully confirmed the details yet but it's likely I will go, particularly after today's discussion [in Kyiv on 24 August].
…I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks."
Details: Burnham made the statement during his first international visit since taking office as prime minister, after he chaired a meeting of Ukraine's allies for the first time and held bilateral talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly appealed to European countries and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot interceptor missiles and replenish its stocks before winter, when Russia is expected to step up attacks on energy infrastructure again. These interceptors are the most powerful weapons available for shooting down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles.
Burnham said he had left Kyiv "really optimistic" that Ukraine's current difficulties in defending itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks, caused by insufficient stocks of interceptors, are "fixable".
He said European leaders were considering holding another meeting of the Coalition of the Willing on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session to secure supplies of US-made interceptors for Ukraine and stocks from other countries.
Quote: "That would seem to be the most likely pace of direction. Not confirmed yet, but that seemed like where most people's minds were going."
Details: Burnham stressed that although the UK does not operate the Patriot missiles Ukraine needs, other European countries should step up their efforts in this area.
Quote: "There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with.
It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."
Previously: Zelenskyy discussed the creation of a European anti-ballistic system with Keith Kellogg, US former special envoy for Ukraine, and reiterated that Patriot interceptors remain indispensable for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy has called on partners to provide Ukraine with missiles for Patriot air defence systems and introduce new sanctions against Russia.
Zelenskyy said earlier that Ukraine needs 5% of the US stockpile of Patriot interceptors to survive the winter and 10% to destroy "all the Russians' ballistic missiles".
Background:
- During his visit to Kyiv, Burnham said London had approved a decision to share Storm Shadow production technology with Ukraine.
- The Kremlin said the UK's decision to hand over secret technology for producing long-range Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles to Ukraine is "adding fuel to the flames".
- Burnham responded to the Kremlin spokesperson's comments on the Russia-Ukraine war.

articles.title: 2 children among 4 killed in Gaza a week after US asked Israel to curb attacks
articles.body:
Strikes in Gaza kill 4, including 2 children, a week after US asked Israel to curb attacks
DEIR AL-BALAH, Gaza Strip (AP) — Palestinian residents of war-battered Gaza fled homes and businesses as Israeli strikes and tank fire killed at least four people Monday, including two children, hospital officials said, a week after a U.S. delegation asked Israel to draw down attacks.
After evacuation warnings by Israel’s military, a strike hit a building in the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza. One family was unable to flee and a 4-year-old child was killed, according to Awda Hospital, where he was taken. His mother and sister were wounded. There was no Israeli military comment.
Israeli strikes hit three other buildings across the territory after residents said they received evacuation warnings. Some people sprinted away, with mothers carrying children, while others moved amid the rubble in wheelchairs or with canes.
Smoke rose over the already devastated landscape.
Israel’s military said it carried out strikes in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City and in Deir al-Balah after issuing warnings, targeting what it described as two Hamas weapons storage facilities inside mosques. The military did not provide evidence but said the facilities contained dozens of “Kalashnikov rifles, magazines and additional military equipment.”
An earlier Israeli strike on a tent in Deir al-Balah killed a man, according to Al-Aqsa Hospital, where his body was taken. Israel’s military said it killed a militant affiliated with Hamas’ special forces unit.
Others were killed or hurt in Khan Younis in the south
A man was killed and five others were wounded in an Israeli strike in Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Nasser Hospital, which received the casualties.
And Israeli tank fire hit an area east of Khan Younis, killing a 10-year-old girl, according to the hospital, where her body was taken.
Israel’s military did not immediately comment on the strike in Khan Younis and said it was not aware of the incident with the child.
Israel has continued to carry out targeted killings in the week since a U.S. delegation met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an effort to push last year’s ceasefire deal forward.
U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner asked Netanyahu to draw down Israel’s attacks in Gaza, a person familiar with the meeting said last week, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief journalists.
Israel has announced strikes on six of the seven days since that meeting.
Israel says it is targeting militants and related sites
While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the ceasefire took hold in October, Israeli airstrikes have killed at least 1,288 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains detailed casualty records that are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Militants have carried out shooting attacks on Israeli troops, and Israel says its strikes are in response to that and other ceasefire violations. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire.
Palestinian officials have reported strikes on homes and police stations, and Hamas has claimed that attacks are designed to destabilize Gaza and prevent progress on the ceasefire’s next steps, which include demilitarizing and reconstructing the territory and the deployment of an international stabilization force.
Israel warns against kites sent from Gaza
In the period before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel that sparked the war, burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into Israel, causing fires and other damage.
Now Israeli officials are expressing concern after several kites were found in a kibbutz near Gaza. No weapons or dangerous materials were attached. Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz in a statement Sunday threatened to ramp up strikes on Gaza unless Hamas ensures the kites stop flying toward Israel.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem has called the kites “essentially children’s toys” and accused Israel of using them as “an attempt to justify the continuation of aggression and violations against our people.”
The Oct. 7 attack killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. All hostages or their remains were later released. Israel’s retaliatory offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,422 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
___
AlJoud reported from Beirut. AP writer Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil tanker in Red Sea
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil tanker in Red Sea
Yemen's Houthis hit a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea with a ballistic missile, as the group pursues a maritime blockade of the kingdom.
"The strike was accurate and direct, resulting in a fire breaking out aboard the vessel and causing a number of other ships that were present in the target area to flee," the Houthis said in a statement.
"This targeting comes as part of the implementation of the Armed Forces' decision to ban maritime navigation by the Saudi enemy."
Saudi Arabia's national shipping company Bahri confirmed on Monday that one of its vessels, the "Amzan", had been attacked in the Red Sea.
"All crew members are safe with no injuries reported," Bahri said in a statement on social media platform X.
Yemen, embroiled in more than a decade of civil conflict, in July became the latest country to be dragged into the Middle East war as the Houthis upended a 2022 truce with the country's Saudi-backed government.
The Houthi claim came hours after a British maritime agency said a tanker struck by an "unknown projectile" caught fire off Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.
"The Company Security Officer reported a tanker has been struck by (an) unknown projectile causing a fire to the vessel on the main deck," said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.
"All crew are safe and accounted for and no environmental impact has been reported," it added.
The incident took place 63 nautical miles west of the Saudi city of Yanbu, the agency reported. Yanbu lies hundreds of kilometres north of Yemen.
British maritime security firm Vanguard Tech also said a Saudi-flagged vessel had been hit by a missile and caught fire.
The Houthis have been attacking the kingdom's ships after declaring last month a maritime blockade of their Saudi foes.
Hostilities erupted in July after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane in Yemen's capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of tit-for-tat attacks.
The Houthis have hit Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and attacked Yemeni government forces since the latest round of fighting broke out.
They have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and airports

articles.title: US widens Iran sanctions as Tehran threatens to halt Gulf oil flows
articles.body:
The United States on Aug. 24 launched a broad economic campaign against Iran, sanctioning nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels and warning third countries that continued dealings with Tehran could expose them to U.S. measures.
Iran responded by threatening to halt oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere in the Persian Gulf if other countries supported Washington’s campaign.
The Treasury Department said Operation Economic Outcast expanded the scope for secondary sanctions in five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington was “entering the endgame” and described the campaign as an “economic D-Day.”
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said.
The campaign puts pressure on governments, companies and financial institutions that continue to facilitate Iranian oil sales or financial transactions.
Bessent accused Iran’s trading partners of buying and transporting its petroleum, channeling funds through exchange houses and free-trade zones, tolerating ship-to-ship fuel transfers and allowing Tehran to use their banking and transport systems.
He said each country had been given a deadline to end activities identified by Washington, without disclosing the time frames. Failure to comply would prompt unilateral action by the Treasury, he added.
Financial institutions found to be facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on Iran’s behalf could also be cut off from the U.S. dollar system.
The Treasury said the latest sanctions targeted networks involved in procuring nuclear and missile technology, a cyber group directed by Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security and oil revenue networks operating through brokers, companies and shadow-fleet vessels.
The networks operated in several jurisdictions, including the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore, Switzerland and Europe, it said.
China, Iran’s largest oil customer, rejected Washington’s pressure campaign. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said sanctions would heighten tensions and serve no one’s interests, urging restraint and a return to dialogue.
Beijing would closely follow developments and take measures to protect its legitimate rights and interests, he added.
Tehran, meanwhile, warned other countries against joining the U.S. campaign.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said that if the economic pressure continued, “not a single drop of oil will be exported” through the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the Persian Gulf.
Iran would regard any country’s participation in or support for Washington’s campaign as “an act of war,” he added.
Iranian lawmakers have also moved forward with plans to charge vessels using the Strait of Hormuz. Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee on Aug. 23 approved a provision allowing fees for navigation, environmental, fuel, insurance, security and other services.
The proposal must still be approved by the full parliament and reviewed by the Guardian Council before it can take effect.

articles.title: Russia will 'try to escalate' against Europe to deter Ukraine support: Macron

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç

Russia will seek to escalate against European countries to deter support for Ukraine, French President Emmanuel Macron warned Monday as European leaders gathered in Kyiv.

“It’s clear that NATO countries will be targeted and the provocations will multiply,” he added, calling for a “robust posture” from European allies.
Macron said France and its partners should accelerate deliveries of air defense interceptors and anti-ballistic missile capabilities to Ukraine.
He warned that shortages of such systems have “direct consequences on people's lives.”
Macron said France would accelerate deliveries of available systems and work with partners to increase production capacity in Ukraine.
He also called for continued support for Ukraine's energy sector ahead of winter and faster disbursement of financial assistance to support the country's budget.
On pressure against Russia, Macron said allies must step up efforts against the so-called shadow fleet used to circumvent sanctions.
 
“We must double down on our efforts regarding sanctions and respective measures and strengthen our coordination,” he said.
Macron proposed a ministerial meeting in the coming weeks focused on measures against the shadow fleet.
He also urged allies to prepare new sanctions targeting Russian oil and gas imports.
Macron said Russia has increasingly turned to imports from third countries following measures against its shadow fleet.
On security guarantees, Macron said the Coalition of the Willing would conduct a full-scale exercise in October and November to demonstrate its operational preparedness and ability to act once hostilities cease.

articles.title: 'Predictable risks': Two more US senators call for independant probe into naval warship conditions
articles.body:
Two additional US senators demanded answers from the Pentagon regarding the living conditions aboard three naval ships involved in the war against Iran.
The letter, shared on Monday by CNN and signed by US Appropriations Committee Vice Chair Patty Murray (Dem. Washington) and Subcommittee on Defense Ranking Member Christopher A. Coons (Dem. Delaware), was addressed to US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao.
Because of the US Department of Defense's "inability, or refusal, to provide the congressional defense committees with full and accurate information," Murray and Coons called on the US Navy to initiate an independent review of the extended deployments and the issues reported onboard the USS Gerald R. Ford, USS Abraham Lincoln, and the USS Benfold.
Senior civilian executives and former military officers should spearhead the investigation, the two said, adding that the review should also "provide recommendations in these areas to improve future extended deployments."
Ford was sent to the Middle East in February 2026, about eight months into her deployment. In March, a laundry fire broke out on the ship, took about 30 hours to extinguish, and injured two service members. She docked in Crete for repairs and returned to the US in May 2026, after more than 300 days at sea.
Benfold, a Flight I Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, went several days without power while deployed in the South China Sea, a US naval spokesperson told CBS News last week, affecting the ship's plumbing, meals, and air conditioning. US officials told CBS that Benfold was being protected by other assets in the region.
Controversy onboard the Lincoln reached its peak two weeks ago, when US military news outlets Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported deteriorating living conditions and worsening mental health among service members. Since then, several letters have been sent to Hegeth and Cao, demanding answers about the reports.
Lincoln is now on her way back to the US after 250 days at sea without making a port call since departing San Diego in November 2025.
Worsening mental health, morale, supply issues
The pair note the reports of mental health and morale concerns aboard the warships, as well as supply issues for basic necessities, long mess hall lines, and disrupted and lost mail service.
"After working long shifts on duty during combat operations, our sailors and Marines should not have to worry about basic day-to-day functions, whether they’ll have a full meal or be able to communicate with their family members," the letter states.
Further, Murray and Coons argue that the US Navy was "inadequately prepared for predictable risks" in the war with Iran, including the availability of relief aircraft carrier groups and disruptions to the naval supply chain in the Middle East.
"We are also concerned about the future unbudgeted maintenance costs for the Ford and Lincoln and the length of time required to complete these repairs," they said, "which have not yet been outlined to Congress despite our requests."
What are US Navy's contingency plans?
Murray and Coons also request to know whether the Lincoln will make a port call during its journey home, what resources will be available to sailors upon their return home, when the final investigation report on Ford's laundry fire will be submitted, and what steps the US Navy is taking to prevent similar issues from happening on the USS George H.W.
Bush, USS George Washington, and other ships deployed to the region. 
Additionally, the two demand to know what the US Navy's contingency plans were for Ford's extended deployment, supply chain disruptions, and military force requirements in the ongoing conflict as Ford and Lincoln undergo repairs.
Murray and Coons granted Hegseth and Cao until September 1 to provide answers and open an independent strategic review into the warships.

articles.title: US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran
articles.body:
The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do.
It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally.
Iran, meanwhile, vowed retaliation against any country that took part in the US-led isolation campaign.
Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.
“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Bessent said on Monday. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
Asked whether sanctions would be applied to China, which bought an estimated 80% of Iran’s shipped oil last year, he replied: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions. That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”
Bessent said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.
“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”
Bessent said Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.
China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem. China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”
Tehran said it would retaliate against the sanctions using a range of measures. Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces’ chief of staff, said the retaliation could take the form of land, sea or air operations or cyber-attacks.
The announcement of secondary sanctions against Iran comes nearly six months after the the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Early expectations that the regime in Tehran would collapse or agree to Washington’s demands to give up uranium enrichment and other key elements of its nuclear programme were dashed.
Hardliners appeared to strengthen their grip on government in Tehran and responded by declaring the closure of the strait of Hormuz, attacking ships that ignored its declaration. Trump imposed a counter-blockage on Iranian oil exports through the strait, leading to an impasse that has had profound effects on the global economy.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.”
The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, however, said further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth told reporters on Monday.
In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions.
Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. But while sanctions can be effective, it is highly unlikely they will produce a quick settlement favourable to the United States.”

articles.title: US urges new UN sanctions to spur rivals in Sudan to negotiate an end to war
articles.body:
US urges new UN sanctions to spur rivals in Sudan to negotiate an end to war
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The United States is urging beefed-up U.N. sanctions against the warring parties in Sudan to build pressure on them to negotiate an end to the fighting that has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced some 13 million and pushed many parts of the African nation into famine.
President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, told the U.N. Security Council on Monday that financial, military and political support given to either the government forces or the rival paramilitary group, Rapid Support Forces, remains a driver of the conflict, now in its fourth year.
Boulos did not name any countries providing that support. Egypt has been a vocal supporter of Sudan’s military, while the United Arab Emirates is accused by U.N. experts and human rights groups of providing arms to the RSF, which it has repeatedly denied.
He said the Security Council has the tools to curtail the provision of “a tremendous and increasing amount of military support to both warring parties” from “numerous external actors.”
U.N.-backed human rights investigators two years ago called for the expansion of an arms embargo on Sudan’s long-restive western Darfur region — scene of mass atrocities between 2003 and 2005 — to cover the entire country.
Boulos said a proposed U.S. resolution before the U.N. Security Council would expand the arms embargo throughout Sudan. It also would apply “to all parties operating in the territory” and reaffirm that drones and related technologies are part of the arms embargo.
Experts say Sudan’s army and the RSF are competing to obtain new drone models. Rights groups have said the use of unmanned aircraft has become increasingly common in the northeast African nation’s war.
The U.S. draft resolution, obtained by The Associated Press, deplores “the continuous influx of external military assistance, weapons, and ammunition to the warring parties, which is prolonging the conflict and undermining mediation efforts,” including launching drones and unmanned aerial systems from third countries.
The proposed resolution demands that all countries “cease any direct or indirect support to the warring parties, be it logistical, financial or military, which enables conflict to continue.”
The conflict exploded from a power struggle that emerged following Sudan’s transition to democracy after an uprising forced the military ouster of longtime autocratic President Omar al-Bashir in April 2019.
Tensions boiled over three years later between Sudan’s military chief Gen. Abdel-Fattah Burhan, who chairs the ruling sovereign council, and RSF commander Gen. Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, who was Burhan’s deputy.
Burhan said Monday that new sanctions would not deter his troops from carrying on with their war until all RSF-controlled areas are captured, according to the army-controlled SUNA news agency.
“Our souls and destiny are in God’s hands,” he said while attending the graduation ceremony of new police officers in the capital, Khartoum. “Our message to those staying in hotels abroad and cheering at sanctions that are meant to subjugate the Sudanese people is the following: The people will not be broken, but we will break and defeat you.”
U.N. political chief Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council that despite numerous diplomatic efforts to get government and paramilitary leaders to start negotiations and end hostilities, “the parties remain locked in a zero-sum military logic.”
“Greater international attention and action are urgently needed for them to change that calculus,” she said.
___
Associated Press writer Noha Elhennawy in Cairo contributed to this report.
