Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro has pitched a 6.3 per cent budget increase to fund the advanced drones and warships
US defence ally the Philippines also planned to acquire additional guided-missile corvettes and other major defence assets to strengthen its external defence capabilities, Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro told a budget hearing in the lower house of Congress.
The armed forces currently operate a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles that provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Teodoro said.
“As we mature on the cycle, then we can acquire more,” Teodoro said in pitching to lawmakers a 6.3 per cent increase in the defence ministry’s budget for 2027, from the 305.5 billion pesos (US$4.95 billion) spending plan approved for this year.
Drone expansion is part of a proposed 50 billion pesos allocation for the Philippines’ modernisation programme next year, 25 per cent higher than that of the current budget.

articles.title: Lawmakers question U.S. Navy’s handling of Iran deployment strain
articles.body:
- Senate Democrats are calling for an Armed Services Committee hearing on extended U.S. Navy deployments tied to operations against Iran.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea more than 250 days, and the USS Gerald R. Ford suffered a fire and plumbing failures during its own extended deployment.
A group of Senate Armed Services Committee Democrats is asking Chairman Roger Wicker to hold a public hearing on extended deployments tied to U.S. military operations against Iran, according to a letter released August 24 by Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).
The letter cites conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which left San Diego on November 21 and has remained at sea for more than 250 days without a scheduled return date. The carrier’s roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines went more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a modern-day record for a U.S. Navy carrier.
Military Times reported August 11 that multiple sailors aboard the Lincoln had attempted to go overboard during the deployment, based on accounts from family members. CNN separately confirmed with U.S. officials that a sailor went overboard on August 3 and was recovered within an hour by a search-and-rescue helicopter, treated aboard ship and transferred for further care. A second overboard incident involving the same strike group occurred last spring, according to a sailor aboard the Lincoln and two U.S. officials who spoke to CNN.
Family members confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at a town hall in San Diego, with one spouse describing a message from her husband saying he hoped he would not wake up the next morning, according to Military Times and Stars and Stripes reporting cited in the letter.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has disputed the Military Times account, calling it “completely misrepresented.” The Navy has said no service members aboard the Lincoln have died and that the August 3 sailor was quickly and safely recovered.
The senators’ letter also points to the USS Gerald R. Ford, which suffered a laundry-room fire on March 12 that took more than 30 hours to extinguish, injured two sailors and damaged roughly 100 sleeping berths. The Navy initially described the fire as contained and said the ship remained fully operational. Later footage obtained by CNN showed more extensive damage, including burned bunks and exposed wiring in crew living spaces.
The Ford left frontline operations and sailed to Souda Bay, Crete, for repairs, then stopped in Split, Croatia, before returning to sea on April 2. The ship had also experienced recurring failures in its roughly 650-toilet vacuum waste system throughout the deployment. The carrier ultimately spent about 11 months at sea, exceeding the Navy’s typical seven-month deployment target, before returning to Norfolk in May for scheduled maintenance.
Both carriers were redirected from other missions to support Iran operations. The Lincoln had been headed for a routine Indo-Pacific patrol before its diversion to the Middle East in January. The Ford was pulled from a planned deployment to Europe, sent briefly to the Caribbean in connection with operations against Venezuela, and then routed to the Middle East.
“The toll this unauthorized, disastrous war is taking on our troops is unconscionable,” the senators wrote, characterizing the military campaign against Iran as illegal and citing what they described as a pattern of inadequate planning for extended deployments.
The senators asked the Armed Services Committee to examine morale conditions, financial strain on military families, and the Department of War’s plan for ending the extended deployments. They also requested that the department detail how it plans to sustain troops in the region if the campaign continues.
The USS George Washington has since been ordered to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official cited by CNN. As of the senators’ letter, no public timeline had been given for the Lincoln’s return to San Diego, and Chairman Wicker had not publicly responded to the hearing request.

articles.title: UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles
articles.body:
UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles
Following his first international visit to Kyiv, the new UK leader seeks a multi-nation deal to secure vital interceptors for Ukraine
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he and other European leaders plan to travel to the US next month to lobby President Donald Trump to let Ukraine access some of its Patriot air defence missile stocks ahead of the winter.
“I’m looking forward to going to New York in September,” Burnham said in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv on Monday evening, referring to the coming UN General Assembly meeting in New York. It would be his first trip to the US since becoming prime minister.
“I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion,” he said. “Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
Burnham’s comments came on his first international visit since becoming premier, after chairing a meeting of Ukraine’s allies for the first time and holding a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky has made repeated pleas to European nations and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot missile interceptors and to replenish its stocks in time for winter, when Russia is expected to ramp up attacks on energy infrastructure again. The interceptors are the most potent weapons to shoot down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles.
Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current struggles defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to its low stockpile of interceptors are “fixable”.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, France back Palestinian state, call for Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanon
articles.body:
Tarek Chouiref
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Saudi Arabia and France reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood and called for Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory, according to a joint statement issued Monday at the end of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s state visit to France.
The statement followed talks between bin Salman and French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris, where they also chaired the first meeting of the Saudi-French Strategic Partnership Council.
The two leaders stressed a shared approach to regional stability based on state sovereignty, international law and political and diplomatic solutions to conflicts.
On Palestine, Riyadh and Paris firmly rejected attempts to undermine the Palestinian people’s right to establish an independent state on the 1967 borders and called for an end to Israel’s settlement policy and violence by Israeli occupiers, saying they threaten the two-state solution.
They also stressed the need to create conditions for a sustainable ceasefire in Gaza and ensure the urgent, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid.
The two sides welcomed the announcement of an agreement on the disarmament of Hamas and called for its implementation while reaffirming their commitment to the New York Declaration and backing Palestinian Authority reforms and plans for presidential and legislative elections.
On Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and France agreed to intensify efforts toward a final settlement, strengthen state institutions and preserve the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
They also called for the full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, the complete disarmament of all armed groups outside state control and Israel’s withdrawal from all Lebanese territory.
The two countries also reaffirmed support for the Lebanese Armed Forces and security agencies.
On Iran, Riyadh and Paris stressed the need for a negotiated solution to prevent further escalation and reiterated support for diplomacy to ensure the peaceful nature of Tehran’s nuclear program.
They also called on Iran to resume full cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency.
The statement also condemned attacks on vessels and threats to navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and called for shipping to return to conditions that existed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, including freedom of navigation and passage without direct or indirect fees or restrictions.
On Syria, the two countries reaffirmed their commitment to the country’s unity, stability and economic recovery, stressing the importance of strong institutions and greater investment.
They welcomed the establishment of a joint Saudi-Syrian-French Business Council and highlighted Syria’s potential to serve as a bridge linking Europe, the Gulf and Asia.
On Yemen, Riyadh and Paris reiterated support for the Presidential Leadership Council and UN efforts toward a comprehensive settlement.
They condemned Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure and vital facilities in Saudi Arabia as well as attacks on commercial shipping while reaffirming their commitment to freedom of navigation.
France also expressed full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and rejected attacks on its territory.
On Sudan, the two sides called for intensified efforts to end the crisis and halt foreign interference while preserving the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and institutions.
Saudi Arabia and France also agreed to deepen defense cooperation, including in armaments and training.
During the visit, the two countries signed agreements and memorandums of understanding covering defense, health, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies and entertainment.
The joint statement said bilateral trade reached about $11.8 billion in 2025, while 21 agreements and memorandums of understanding were announced during a Saudi-French investment roundtable.
The Aug. 23-24 visit came as Saudi Arabia and France marked 100 years since the establishment of political relations.

articles.title: US strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months
articles.body:
The US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking.
On Monday, US Southern Command (SouthCom) announced it “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”.
“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed two narco-terrorists,” SouthCom added.
Southern Command did not provide evidence for the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking.
In a statement on the strikes, Francis L Donovan, SouthCom’s commander general, said: “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”
“This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the US homeland,” Donovan added.
A pixelated black-and-white video posted to SouthCom’s X account on Monday showed a vessel moving through the water before it was struck by an explosion that produced a large flash of light.
Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series of US military strikes since the Donald Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US, despite numerous reports indicating that the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country.
It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft.
The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.
Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.
The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered.
US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful.
According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia.
The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws.
Despite the defense department framing the strikes as attacks against “narco-terrorism”, it has provided little evidence on whether the vessels were actually transporting drugs. The attacks have been condemned as extrajudicial killings by the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations.
According to a 2020 report by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, 74% of the cocaine reaching the US arrived through the Pacific while only 8% came from fast boats from the Caribbean.
Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.
The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.
Meanwhile, an investigation by the Latin American Center for Investigative Journalism (Clip) this year identified 13 previously unidentified victims of US vessel attacks. All came from impoverished communities across Latin America and the Caribbean and several were fishers with no indication of involvement in the drug trade, it found.
“There are communities where they stopped fishing for several weeks – and if they do that, people go hungry – because they were terrified of being bombed,” María Teresa Ronderos, Clip director, said at the time of the report’s release.
Other families continue to grieve as they seek answers about their relatives killed in US airstrikes.
“If the boat was carrying so much cocaine and then exploded and caught fire, where is the evidence? Where is the cocaine? That is what I want to know. I know Ricky. He was a fisherman. That was his life,” Titus, the brother of Ricky Joseph, one of the 13 people identified in the CLIP investigation, said in June from the Carribean island of St Lucia.

articles.title: Ukraine holds 1st-ever drone parade on 35th Independence Day
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The Ukrainian capital Kyiv hosted the country’s first-ever parade of aerial, ground and maritime drones Monday as the nation marked its 35th Independence Day, the presidential press service said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is now able to share technologies developed during the war with Russia to help protect its partners.
“Today we will see Ukrainian might. What we use to protect the lives of our people. What is making this war special right now, and what will allow Ukraine, after this war, to become a true security donor for its partners, its friends, and our Europe and everyone who has helped us,” he said. “Ukraine knows how to be grateful.”
According to the statement, 30 ground robotic systems traveled along Khreshchatyk Street, including TerMIT, Rys, Simba, Ardal, Zmiy and Ratel, which are designed to reduce risks to Ukrainian troops.
Nine Ukrainian unmanned boats, developed and tested in combat during the war, traveled along the Dnipro River.
The Sea Baby, Magura and Sargan platforms conduct reconnaissance and patrol missions, strike maritime targets and launch drones.
Eighteen P1-Sun, Litavr and Sting aerial interceptors, developed to combat Iranian-designed Shahed drones and other types of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), flew over Kyiv, followed by 27 bomber drones, including the Vampire, Lazar and Heavy Shot.
Eight reconnaissance drones, including SHARK and LF-400, also took part.
The parade concluded with seven Morok and Sichen drones designed for long-range strikes.

articles.title: US can still strike Hormuz targets, Hegseth warns as 'Economic D-Day' takes aim at Iran's economy
articles.body:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Monday that US President Donald Trump's administration was not ruling out using military force against Iran, even as Washington unveiled an "economic D-Day" against Tehran.
"By no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran," Hegseth told reporters, adding that Iran could not handle the economic pressure being put on it.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the start of "Operation Economic Outcast" on Iran in remarks at a press conference on Monday following earlier threats of an "economic D-Day" against the regime.
"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.
Bessent described the operation as "a sustained campaign to collapse every last option for Iran," saying that those involved in "any" economic cooperation with Tehran would expose themselves to "the full reach of American power."
'Economic Outcast' to last until Iran 'stands alone,' Bessent said
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US Dollar system," he emphasized. "the clock just started ticking."
He further warned against any nation "testing" the resolve of the US government.
"It is now a time for world leaders to make a decision between prosperity and isolation, peace and terror, America and Iran," he declared.
Bessent concluded his remarks by noting that Operation Economic Outcast would continue until Iran "stands alone."
Iran won't have nuclear weapon, State Dept. spox. maintains
Trump is still set on preventing Iran from attaining a nuclear bomb, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a Newsmax interview on Monday afternoon.
"The president has been clear that he is going to see the Iranian nuclear weapons threat come to an end," he said, adding that "He will see that objective be completed one way or another."

articles.title: US vows 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran with new sanctions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US vows 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran with new sanctions
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, expanding Washington's secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.
The announcement comes almost six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate, with stalled peace talks and Tehran blocking most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Bessent earlier said the US was declaring an "economic D-Day" on Iran, but his announcement named no specific countries beyond Iran and gave no timelines.
"Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent told journalists.
"We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime."
He added that countries not joining US sanctions would "share in the isolation" of Iran, and noted that President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with requests to stop interactions with Tehran.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyber operations.
The sanctions hit entities around the world, including in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and in Europe.
Bessent vowed that any entity "that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system."
Iran had been dismissive of the threat of additional sanctions, and on Monday its economy minister predicted "another defeat" for Washington.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," said Ali Madanizadeh.
Decades of sanctions
Iran has weathered decades of crushing international sanctions, and before the war it continued to export millions of barrels of oil, mostly to China, and to evade sanctions through complex international financial networks.
Asked on Monday if Chinese banks would be targeted by the new sanctions, Bessent said "no one is above the reach of US sanctions."
Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group said Washington was seeking to impose maximum economic pressure through various levers, but that Iran "has faced all of these before."
"While there is little doubt in Washington's ability to impose substantial pain, Tehran believes that it has a high threshold for absorbing it, as well as the potential to respond to financial pressure with military counterpressure," he said.
The US naval blockade of Iran has seen its oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz fall from two million barrels a day pre-war to just 0.4 million by mid-August, according to maritime tracker Kpler.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the pivot to applying economic pressure did not mean that military strikes were off the table.
"Economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now," he said. "But by no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran."
For ordinary Iranians, the standoff is likely to bring only more economic pain after years of rampant inflation, which in December and January fueled massive anti-government protests.
Sarah Hassanbeigi, a 32-year-old pharmacist in Tehran, said: "I don't think people can really take this much longer."
Pakistani delegation
Last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, considered a relative moderate, said Tehran should "bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power."
That followed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's appointment of hardliners to key security positions.
On Monday, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir -- a key mediator in the conflict -- visited Iran and met separately with Iran's president, chief negotiator and the head of its highest national security body.
The meetings took place after Trump spoke last week with Munir, a US source familiar with the matter told AFP earlier on Monday.
Islamabad was a leading mediator in talks that helped secure an April ceasefire that later fell apart. It is also a major trading partner of Iran, possibly opening it up to the threat of the new sanctions.
Oman's foreign minister was due in Iran on Tuesday, as Muscat and Tehran seek a deal on regulating passage through Hormuz.

articles.title: Tehran warns countries supporting US military actions of consequences
articles.body:
Tehran warns countries supporting US military actions of consequences
TEHRAN — Iran warned on Monday that countries allowing the United States or Israel to use their military bases, facilities or equipment for operations against Iran could face consequences, as Tehran hardened its position over the ongoing regional crisis and rejected any attempt to end the conflict on terms dictated by its adversaries.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Iran’s diplomatic strategy was being adjusted to reflect changing regional and international conditions, while emphasizing that Tehran would continue using bilateral and multilateral channels to defend what it considers its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at his weekly press conference in Tehran, Baqaei said Iran could not rely on diplomatic methods developed under different circumstances and needed to continuously strengthen its diplomatic capabilities. He described the US campaign of economic pressure as “economic warfare” and said Tehran had repeatedly characterized such measures as economic terrorism.
The spokesperson said Washington was using multiple forms of pressure against Iranians because of their insistence on national sovereignty, independence and dignity. He warned that Iran had already issued, and would continue to issue, warnings concerning countries that cooperate with US actions against the Islamic Republic.
Tehran rejects war settlement dictated by aggressor
The Iranian spokesman also sought to clarify President Masoud Pezeshkian’s recent comments that it would be preferable to end the war while Iran was in a position of strength.
Baqaei rejected interpretations that the remarks indicated Tehran was prepared to make concessions to its adversaries. He said Iran had not initiated the conflict and would not permit the war to end on conditions imposed by the party responsible for the aggression.
“We will show no leniency toward the aggressors,” Baqaei said, arguing that Iran had been defending its territorial integrity and national sovereignty. He added that the aggressor should be held accountable.
According to Baqaei, the Iranian leadership had repeatedly made clear that the country would not surrender to coercion or domination. He said the government and all branches of the Iranian state had acted with unity during the 40-day conflict as well as during an earlier 12-day war.
The remarks underscore Tehran’s insistence that any future diplomatic process must take place without what it regards as coercive demands from Washington or its allies.
The spokesman also criticized the United States for what he described as repeated breaches of commitments in previous negotiations, including the 2015 nuclear agreement and other diplomatic understandings. He said Iran had repeatedly responded to what it considered goodwill gestures from Tehran with broken promises.
Warning to countries providing bases
Baqaei issued one of his strongest warnings to countries whose military infrastructure could be used by the United States or Israel in operations against Iran.
Responding to reports concerning American military facilities and aircraft in European countries, he said Tehran had previously made clear its position on Bulgaria and confirmed reports that several US KC-135 refueling aircraft had departed the country.
Baqaei argued that allowing foreign military forces to use national bases and facilities for attacks on Iran could amount to participation in aggression under international law. He said Iran had no dispute with the people of Bulgaria but viewed the use of facilities there in support of US and Israeli military operations as problematic.
He further warned that Iran considered itself entitled to respond against the source of an attack.
“It is Iran’s right to target the source and origin of any act of aggression,” Baqaei said, adding that Tehran would show no leniency in defending the country.
The warning comes amid heightened sensitivity over the role of foreign military bases and logistical facilities in any potential resumption of hostilities.
Strait of Hormuz becomes a key flashpoint
The Strait of Hormuz was another major focus of the briefing, with Baqaei rejecting claims in US media and official circles that the strategic waterway had become fully open to shipping.
He disputed reports citing oil flows ranging from 5 million to 17 million barrels per day and claims of a sharp increase in maritime traffic. Baqaei described the figures as part of what he called a media and psychological campaign, arguing that insecurity created by US and Israeli actions had affected conditions in the region and around the strait since February 28, 2026.
The comments highlight the strategic importance of Hormuz, through which a significant share of global energy supplies normally passes, and signal that Tehran continues to regard security and traffic through the waterway as closely linked to the wider regional conflict.
Baqaei said Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi, who was scheduled to visit Tehran, would discuss bilateral relations as well as security and shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, he rejected suggestions that the Omani visit was connected to the simultaneous visit by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.
Diplomacy continues amid economic pressure
Despite the confrontational rhetoric, Tehran said diplomatic engagement with neighboring countries remained active.
Baqaei described relations with Pakistan as being at their strongest stages and said Munir’s visit was aimed at further expanding bilateral ties. He also pointed to efforts to improve economic relations with Afghanistan, including reducing border and customs barriers.
He said a meeting between Afghan Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Mullah Baradar and President Pezeshkian had addressed ways of facilitating economic cooperation, adding that measures to remove obstacles to trade had subsequently been placed on the agenda.
Iran is also dealing with the consequences of US economic pressure and damage to its energy infrastructure. Baqaei said the government was taking the necessary measures to meet winter energy requirements, with the Oil Ministry handling technical preparations and the Foreign Ministry engaging with countries capable of supplying energy if needed.
He accused Washington of seeking to undermine Iran’s sovereignty while also damaging the international free-trade system by pressuring other countries to restrict commerce with Tehran. He called such pressure a violation of international relations and the principles of the U.N. Charter.
Tehran maintains regional policy
Baqaei also reaffirmed Iran’s opposition to Israel’s occupation and military presence in the region, describing resistance to what Tehran calls Zionist occupation as a principled element of Iranian foreign policy.
He said Iran’s position was not dependent on which political group or faction governed other Islamic countries and reiterated Tehran’s opposition to what it described as continued Israeli occupation and aggression in Syria.
At the same time, Baqaei denied reports that Iran had received an official invitation to join a proposed trilateral defense arrangement involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. He said regional proposals presented to Tehran so far had centered on dialogue, consultations and collective security rather than formal membership in a new defense bloc.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Putin Talked Greatness for 27 Years—Now Russia is Queuing for Gas
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Zelenskyy: Putin Talked Greatness for 27 Years—Now Russia is Queuing for Gas
Ukraine will not surrender its territory to Russia or ease the enormous military cost Moscow is paying for its invasion, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a defiant Independence Day address on August 24.
Zelenskyy rejected the idea that handing over Donbas could quickly end Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, arguing that the Kremlin continues to misjudge both Ukraine’s willingness and its ability to resist.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Putin is stuck in the past. He still looks at an old-style Ukraine—one that will stay silent, swallow it, endure it,” Zelenskyy said.
“That Ukraine exists nowhere anymore, except in his ‘little folders of reports.’ Our state has long been different. Not an observer, but a player. Not a victim, but a fighter.”
The Ukrainian leader said Kyiv would not allow Russia to regain the initiative or convince Ukraine’s partners that territorial concessions could provide a shortcut to peace.
“We will not let them seize the initiative, deceive Europe and the entire world into thinking that they simply need to give up Donbas, and everything will be over soon,” the President said.
Zelenskyy said there were no grounds for trusting such Russian promises and made clear that Ukraine would continue resisting rather than effectively rescuing Moscow from further battlefield losses.
“We have no illusions. We don’t trust them. We are not going to save the Kremlin half a million soldiers,” according to Zelenskyy.
He pointed to Russia’s repeatedly delayed ambitions to capture the entirety of Ukraine’s Donetsk region as evidence that Moscow’s military plans continue to fall short of its own timelines.
“Russia keeps pushing back the dates when they will ‘definitely, any day now, take the entire Donetsk region.’ It will keep pushing those dates back. Ukraine is different, and it does not give away what is its own,” he stated.
Zelenskyy also said Russia was preparing for another wave of mobilization rather than genuinely seeking an end to the war. For Ukraine, he said, the response must be to strengthen its military and ensure frontline troops have the weapons and equipment necessary to maintain the defense.
“We have to strengthen our military, have everything needed to hold our defense. Our warriors must be supplied and equipped with everything so that the replenishment of the enemy army can be turned into fertilizer for our soil.”
Zelenskyy ended his Independence Day address by directly challenging the expectations of Russian leader Vladimir Putin and contrasting Moscow’s original ambitions with the losses Russia has suffered during more than four years of full-scale war.
“Putin hopes that we are tired. But we know that he is mortal. He never understood us. Now he will not have time to. You wanted to take all our Ukraine, all our land; instead, you lost your oil refineries, your fleet, your profits, your entire generation that you sent into the meat grinder. You wanted us erased from the map; now you are absent from the international agenda of the future civilization,” he said.
Zelenskyy also pointed out the image of power the Kremlin has spent decades trying to project.
“For 27 years, the head of Russia has talked about greatness, while Russia is standing in lines for gasoline,” he concluded.
Earlier, reports emerged that fuel availability at Russian gas stations has plunged sharply, with gasoline reportedly available at only 28.1% of stations nationwide as authorities open dozens of antitrust cases against oil companies and independent fuel operators.

Ukraine Torches Three Ozon Mega-Warehouses, Hits MiG-29, as Drone Forces Hit 66 Targets in One Night
Ukrainian strike drones hit three major Ozon logistics centers across southern Russia, igniting large fires at facilities with a combined warehouse area of more than 314,000 square meters, according to photos and videos published by the OSINT community Exilenova+ on August 24.
The strikes formed part of a much broader Ukrainian operation deep behind Russian lines. Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said his units successfully engaged 66 Russian targets during the night, including a MiG-29 fighter jet, four radar systems, military facilities and vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Birds of the Unmanned Systems Forces successfully struck 66 enemy targets in the operational depth of the enemy rear on the night of August 24,” Brovdi said.
Among the most significant targets, according to the commander, was another Russian MiG-29 near Dolotinka in Russia’s Rostov region.
“Among the sensitive targets was another MiG-29 [Dolotinka, Rostov region, Russia] and four radar systems: two Kasta-2E2 units, a Nebo-SV radar [all in Russia’s Rostov region] and an ST-68 radar [Rozdolne, Crimea],” Brovdi said.
He also reported the destruction of a base used by Russia’s SOBR special police forces in occupied Strilkove in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as strikes against energy infrastructure across Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.
Two vessels associated with Russia’s shadow fleet—a tanker and a bulk carrier—were also hit in the Black Sea, Brovdi said. Eleven Russian temporary deployment points were struck across occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Three Ozon logistics centers were among the most visible targets of the overnight campaign.
The largest was a warehouse complex near Tyube in Russia’s Dagestan region, covering approximately 130,000 square meters. The site serves as a major logistics hub for northern Dagestan and lies roughly 800 to 900 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
A major fire erupted following the strike, with local residents reporting that the glow from the blaze could be seen from as far as 10 kilometers away.
Another Ozon logistics center was targeted in Nevinnomyssk, in Russia’s Stavropol region. The facility covers approximately 93,514 square meters.
The third site was an Ozon warehouse near Enem in Adygea, close to the border with Russia’s Krasnodar region. The complex covers about 91,200 square meters. A large fire developed at the facility after the attack.
Ozon is one of Russia’s largest online marketplaces and operates a sprawling logistics network comparable in function to major Western e-commerce platforms.
An investigation earlier found that Russian troops fighting in Ukraine had repeatedly ordered body armor, thermal-imaging equipment, radios, drone batteries, signal boosters, FPV components and payload-release systems through Ozon. Drone-related products were ordered through Ozon particularly frequently.
Ukraine has already put seven of the ten largest logistics centers operated by Russian e-commerce company Wildberries, OZON rival, out of operation.
Wildberries facilities in Domodedovo and at the Koledino industrial park were among the sites affected. The Koledino facility, covering approximately 250,000 square meters, was the company’s largest warehouse by area.

articles.title: Ontario’s premier: Canada should be ready to cut electricity, critical minerals as trade woes worsen
articles.body:
Canada to announce retaliatory tariffs as Trump tells its leaders to ‘fall in line’
TORONTO (AP) — Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday after relations deteriorated sharply Monday, with President Donald Trump telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs and Prime Minister Mark Carney accusing Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.
Trump also threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, while Carney said U.S. trade demands showed Washington wanted to “destroy our major industries,” including autos, steel and aluminum.
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are also expected Tuesday morning to share details of supports for workers affected by tariffs. Carney said earlier Monday that Canada may need to move away from matching U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar and instead use more targeted retaliation aimed at protecting Canadian workers and businesses.
“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said.
Carney was even more blunt in French.
“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”
The fiery words from both sides show how U.S.-Canada relations have deteriorated since Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, triggering the president’s threatened 50% tariffs the next day on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Canada and the United States share one of the world’s largest trading relationships, with deeply integrated supply chains across autos, energy, agriculture and manufacturing, making a prolonged trade fight potentially costly for businesses and workers on both sides of the border.
Carney cast doubt on the U.S.’s dependability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.”
Trump unleashes personal attacks on Canadian leaders
On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada’s auto industry beginning next year.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticizing what he called the country’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.
Carney said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production.
“This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-U.S. industry.
Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure.
“We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”
Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and once again referring to Canada’s prime minister as “Governor Carney.”
Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.”
Ford is a Progressive Conservative whose party differs from that of Carney, a Liberal, but the two underscore broad political unity in Canada over the trade fight with Trump.
Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity
Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario.
Critical minerals are increasingly important to U.S. national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.
Ford said Canada should also consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south.
“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”
Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides backed away.
Auto industry becomes a central battleground
Ford accused Trump of not simply seeking a better trade deal but aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.
Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state.
“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said.
The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the center of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other U.S. states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production.
Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump’s new threat of a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the center of the escalating dispute.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
Ford says he opposed preliminary deal
Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from negotiations, and that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement.
“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.”
Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty.
Carney said the dispute also exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, saying protections for French and Canadian culture that Washington views as trade irritants are considered fundamental rights in Canada.
“Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”
___
Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed from Washington.

articles.title: US snubs joint UN rebuke of Russian strikes against Ukraine — again

The U.S. did not join an Aug. 24 appeal by over 50 U.N. members urging Russia to halt its aggression against Ukraine and cease strikes against civilians.
The statement, backed by the EU and its member states, as well as the U.K., Canada, Japan, South Korea, Georgia, Australia, and others, urged "Russia to respond to the calls for a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire" and resume peace talks.

"Russia simply needs to accept the unconditional ceasefire that Ukraine and the international community have been calling for for over a year and a half now."
Dan Negrea, a U.S. envoy to the United Nations Economic and Social Council, did not sign off on the appeal during the Security Council meeting, instead calling upon "both sides" to cease any strikes that might pose a risk to civilian vessels.
Russia has increasingly targeted Ukrainian Black Sea ports and merchant ships to choke off the country's export routes, while Kyiv has been striking Russia's shadow fleet vessels helping Moscow dodge international sanctions.
Negrea also urged Kyiv and Moscow to go back to the negotiating table and "return peace and stability to both countries," stopping short of condemning Russian aggression.
Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office last year, Washington has refrained from denouncing Russia's invasion and has ceased nearly all military aid to Ukraine in the name of pursuing peace talks — an effort that has effectively stalled as Moscow continues to reject a ceasefire.
The Trump administration has also repeatedly opted out of joint appeals condemning Russian aggression at international forums. In May, the U.S. did not support a rebuke of Russia's threats to foreign embassies in Kyiv.

articles.title: Israel steps up attacks on Syria hours after top Syrian diplomat meets Mossad chief
articles.body:
Israel steps up attacks on Syria hours after top Syrian diplomat meets Mossad chief
TEHRAN — Before dawn on Monday, six Israeli armored vehicles and an infantry company crossed into western Daraa, sweeping homes in the Syrian village of Ma’ariya under hovering surveillance drones before withdrawing back across the occupied Golan frontier.
Hours later, another Israeli unit moved into southern Quneitra, raiding the village of Sayd al-Hanout after detaining a local shepherd near al-Rafid the day before. The ground advances coincided with a blast near Palmyra’s regional directorate.
The raids unfolded hours after the top diplomat of the Ahmad “al-Jolani” al-Sharaa government, Asaad al-Shaibani, sat across from Mossad Director Roman Gofman in Jordan, according to reports from Axios and AFP.
The U.S.-mediated meeting was advertised as an effort to lower regional temperatures following an August 18 Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib.
Instead, the rapid sequence of military operations demonstrated the stark reality on the ground: the so-called diplomatic negotiations in Amman have done nothing to halt Israeli troop movements inside Syria.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights documented seven Israeli ground incursions across Daraa and Quneitra within a single 24-hour window on Monday.
Local monitors counted over 60 military violations between August 15 and August 21 alone, ranging from land-leveling and surveillance camera installations to makeshift military checkpoints.
Rather than isolated raids, these operations form a continuous campaign to carve out operational freedom deep inside Syrian territory.
Air operations follow the same aggressive logic. The August 18 attack on Abu al-Duhur involved eight separate waves of strikes targeting runways and storage facilities.
Israeli officials claimed the strike pre-empted a Turkish military buildup at the base. Both Ankara and Damascus denied the existence of any such deployment, while U.S. Special Envoy Tom Barrack called the bombing “an unnecessary escalation.”
Yet, days after briefly announcing a pause in contacts over the incident, al-Shaibani traveled to Jordan to discuss a proposed U.S.-supervised special operations room supposedly meant to deconflict Israeli, Turkish, and Syrian military movements.
Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has framed the new political reality in Damascus as a strategic opportunity.
Tel Aviv unilaterally voided the 1974 disengagement agreement, seized Mount Hermon, and established forward outposts in the buffer zone.
Roughly 80 percent of subsequent Israeli air strikes have hit Quneitra, Daraa, and Damascus, aiming to keep Syria’s military infrastructure dismantled.
Accommodation has brought the “al-Jolani” al-Sharaa government no security.
In Jordan, the Syrian side reportedly insisted on a full Israeli withdrawal to pre-December 2024 lines and reaffirmed its right to rebuild a national army.
Tel Aviv treats negotiations as a stall tactic to solidify its presence on the ground, while Washington brokers talks without placing boundaries on Israel’s aggressive maneuvers.

articles.title: New details but no answers a year after an Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital killed journalists
articles.body:
New details but no answers a year after an Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital killed journalists
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — It’s been a year since Israeli soldiers killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and rescue workers, in a double strike on a hospital in Gaza. No one has been held accountable.
Israeli officials said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof of Nasser Hospital. Among those killed were Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for The Associated Press and other news organizations.
Despite repeated requests by AP, the army has not provided details about the investigation or a timeline for when it could be completed. Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution.
As global outrage over the Aug. 25, 2025, strike grew, the Israeli military said that in addition to taking out the camera, six of those killed were linked to Hamas, without providing evidence.
But an Israeli soldier, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution, now says the military could find no evidence linking the camera, which belonged to al-Masri, to Hamas. The soldier, who was privy to discussions surrounding the military’s response, said none of the six was the intended target of the strike.
AP sent detailed questions to the military about the allegations, as well as other questions about the strikes. The military didn’t address the questions but said via text that the incident is being examined and findings will be transferred to the Military Advocate General’s Corps to reach a verdict on whether to open a criminal investigation. It didn’t provide a timeline.
AP reported at the time that one of the six Israel said was linked to Hamas was not on the hospital’s list of casualties and two others were medical or emergency personnel. That, along with the soldier’s account, raises serious questions about Israel’s rationale for the strike.
Why did troops fail to identify the cameraman as al-Masri, even though journalists were known to film at the hospital? Why did they strike a second time, causing most of the deaths and raising accusations of a “double tap” attack on first responders, which would be a war crime?
“A year later, we remain devastated by their deaths and are still searching for answers from the Israeli authorities about what happened that day,” AP Executive Editor Julie Pace said.
“The information we have received to date has fallen short of the clear answers and accountability that an incident of this gravity requires.”
Nasser Hospital was a vital location for journalists
News agencies like Reuters and AP supplied live video footage to newsrooms around the world from the hospital, one of the few functioning in Gaza at the time. AP repeatedly informed the army that its journalists were stationed there.
The first strike killed al-Masri and another person. As other journalists, including Dagga, and rescue workers rushed up an external staircase to help the wounded and document what happened, the military struck again, killing 20 people. Based on footage and multiple eyewitnesses, none was armed. In all, Israel struck the hospital four times using high-explosive tank shells.
Israeli officials afterward said Hamas was using the camera to observe nearby troops. They alleged “suspicious behavior” around the camera, but the only example they gave was that a towel draped over the camera and the person filming appeared to be an effort at concealment.
The Reuters journalist, al-Masri, routinely covered equipment with a white cloth to protect it from the sun and dust, a common practice among videojournalists in Gaza and other hot climates.
Last week, the army announced criminal investigations into two other high-profile attacks by its troops in Gaza — the 2024 killing of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, and the 2025 killing of 15 paramedics. It cleared troops in three other attacks that killed workers from international aid groups.
Soldier details an attempt at damage control
The soldier was connected to AP through Breaking the Silence, a group founded over two decades ago by Israeli veterans that collects testimony from soldiers and is critical of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territories.
The soldier said that after high-profile strikes that kill civilians without clear military purpose, army officials retroactively search for militant links among those killed.
Breaking the Silence said its testimonies show there is a “retroactive incrimination process” in which Palestinians who are killed are automatically counted as militants, even when unarmed.
Retroactive incrimination is used as a “near automatic justification for every bullet, shell or missile fired, and as a tool used to avoid carrying out real investigations,” Nadav Weiman, the group’s executive director, said.
AP independently confirmed some details of the soldier’s account, which is consistent with the military’s public response. Breaking the Silence said it had corroborated the account with its own sources.
The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals throughout the war, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters, though it’s provided evidence for only some of its claims.
Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. Earlier this year, Doctors Without Borders suspended some operations at Nasser Hospital for several months after patients and staff reported seeing armed, masked men roaming parts of the building.
Tank shells were fired after a drone failed
The soldier, and a former military official with knowledge of the situation, said a high-ranking army official initially approved use of a precision weapon to take down the camera but an attempt by drone failed for unknown reasons. The former official spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to talk to the media.
The division commander then approved an alternative method, said the soldier, without saying what the method was. It’s unclear who made the decision to fire tank rounds, which can cause more extensive damage than drone strikes.
Oded Ailam, former head of the counterterrorism division in Israel’s Mossad spy service, said that while commanders on the ground have a degree of freedom, they don’t have a “blank check.”
“If the change is significant, particularly where it may affect the risk to civilians, it must remain within the authority, rules and intent of the original order, or require renewed approval,” he said.
Israeli troops have killed over 200 journalists in the war
Israeli troops have killed 207 Palestinian reporters in Gaza since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack ignited the war, according to the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists. Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering Gaza, giving Palestinian journalists a critical role in covering the conflict.
Sara Qudah, CPJ’s Middle East and North Africa regional director, said Israel has a responsibility to conduct a prompt and transparent investigation. “When journalists can be killed without credible accountability, it becomes harder and more dangerous for the press to document conflicts and for the public to know what is happening,” she said.
The lack of answers has been agonizing for the families.
Ezz al-Din al-Masri said he doesn’t understand why his brother, Hussam, was killed. “Unfortunately, we found that the blood of journalists in Gaza is cheap … as if the rules protecting journalists do not apply to them,” he said.
Dagga, 33, had just taken her last photos before rushing up the stairs. Whenever her father, Riyad Abu Dagga, visits her grave, he carries her phone and camera with him — she always had them with her. He visits her apartment near Nasser Hospital and cries.
“Had any of the daughters of the soldiers been killed unjustly, they would not have stayed silent,” he said of the Israelis. “They would want to know why.”
___
AP reporter Wafaa Shurafa in Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
articles.body:
Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Drug gangs and rebel groups in Colombia are increasingly recruiting children and using them to perform potentially lethal tasks that include piloting explosives-laden drones, Human Rights Watch said in a report published Monday.
The international watchdog said criminal organizations in the South American country often use social media to recruit children as they try to assert control over rural areas where they profit from the drug trade, extortion and illegal mining.
“Armed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “Protection systems are failing, and social media platforms have become a more effective recruiting ground.”
Child recruitment is on the rise again
According to Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ Office, at least 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups since 2021, with 625 cases reported in 2024.
In 1999, during the peak of the conflict between Colombia’s military and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, an estimated 1,320 children were recruited into the fighting, according to a report by a national truth commission.
A 2016 peace deal between Colombia’s government and the FARC rebels reduced violence in many parts of the country and slowed the recruitment of children by armed groups.
But child recruitment is picking up again as smaller rebel groups and other criminal organizations fight over control of rural areas abandoned by FARC guerrillas following the peace deal, where law enforcement and social services continue to be weak.
In Colombia, rebel groups have long used children to perform tasks that include serving as messengers, gathering intelligence, cooking or engaging with the enemy — while girls are sometimes forced into sexual acts with commanders.
The Human Rights Watch report says children are now also being trained in drone warfare, as rebel groups increasingly use drones outfitted with explosives to strike at rival groups or launch attacks on police and army bases.
Human Rights Watch verified videos published on social media that show children using explosives-laden drones, and interviewed family protection officers who work with children who have escaped from armed groups or have been allowed to demobilize.
“Released children who report having operated drones say that armed groups describe the activity as a game rather than as participation in armed fighting,” the report said.
Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ office said in a separate report published Monday that armed groups conducted 121 attacks with drones in the first five months of this year, in which 21 people were killed and 145 were injured.
Social media accounts ‘glorify’ life with rebels
Human Rights Watch identified dozens of social media accounts that “glorify” life in rebel groups, echoing a concern previously voiced by the United Nations.
The watchdog group said in some cases, the algorithms of platforms like Meta and TikTok “appear to have actively promoted” such content that encourages children to join rebel groups.
Meta and TikTok replied to Human Rights Watch saying they prohibit content that promotes violence, and that they had taken down accounts flagged by the organization.
Human Rights Watch also said a FARC holdout group led by a commander known as Ivan Mordisco is involved in most cases of child recruitment and is recruiting heavily in Colombia’s Cauca region.
Nearly half of all recruiting cases reported by Colombian authorities since 2021 involved Indigenous children, according to data analysis by Human Rights Watch, despite Indigenous people making up just 4% of the population.
The watchdog group also said girls made up 40% of all recruited children.
Human Rights Watch called on the Colombian government to devote more resources to prosecuting members of armed groups who recruit children, while stepping up efforts to prevent recruitment in rural areas.
There was no immediate government response to the report.
The organization also called on social media platforms to establish channels where users can easily report content that’s related to the recruitment of children, and preserve evidence that can be made available to prosecutors.
___

articles.title: Uganda's Gaza 'stabilisation force' plan sparks debate in Africa
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Uganda's participation in Gaza 'stabilisation force' sparks debate in Africa
Uganda's parliament approved the deployment of army troops to the" International Stabilisation Force" in the Gaza Strip at the beginning of August as part of US President Donald Trump's plan. The move marks the first official declaration by an African country of its readiness to participate in Gaza.
The approval came on 6 August after Ugandan Defence Minister Kiria Kiwanuka told lawmakers that Trump had asked President Yoweri Museveni in July for Uganda to contribute to the proposed international force in Gaza.
After the Ugandan parliament's approval, a Ugandan soldier in military uniform posted a video on social media in which he appeared alongside the words, "Gaza, we are coming", indicating that the idea of a military deployment had begun circulating within Uganda's military and media circles.
The Ugandan government has not yet specified the number of troops it may deploy to the territory or when they would be sent.
Israel's public broadcaster reported last Monday, 17 August, that senior officers from Uganda and Burundi had arrived at the US command headquarters in Kiryat Gat in the occupied Palestinian territories as part of advanced talks with the two countries to send hundreds of soldiers to the territory as part of the multinational stabilisation force.
The broadcaster also said last Thursday, 20 August, that Morocco had been chosen to train members of the force.
Ugandan forces in the Gaza stabilisation force has sparked debate inside the Ugandan parliament, with opposition lawmakers calling for more information about the nature of the mission, the number of troops, its funding, and the guarantees provided to soldiers and their families.
The opposition also warned of the security and political risks associated with sending troops to a devastated territory and under highly complex field conditions.
Uganda has extensive experience in peacekeeping operations, particularly in Africa, where its forces participate in missions in Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The defence minister cited this experience to justify the Ugandan army's ability to participate in a new international mission.
Without African backing
The decision has also raised questions about Kampala's approval of it and whether it has broad African backing or bypasses African consensus by being taken without Uganda consulting its partners in the African Union.
The African Union has consistently supported the Palestinian cause in principle and calls for the implementation of a two-state solution.
However, Israel has built relations with several African countries over decades, viewing the continent as an arena of Arab-Israeli competition.
In 2021, the union accepted Israel as an "observer member", a move that prompted Palestinian and Arab protests and was later revoked.
Uganda's relations with Israel, meanwhile, have continued to grow.
The Ugandan judge Julia Sebutinde, vice-president of the International Court of Justice, has attracted attention after she was described as believing that "God relies on her to stand with Israel". Sebutinde opposed the six rulings imposed by the court in 2024 to protect Palestinians and stop the genocide in Gaza.
Ugandan military leadership also recently said that any attempts to "destroy" Israel, amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, could prompt Uganda to intervene in support of the occupying state.
Uganda is also one of the largest importers of military technology and spyware from the occupying state.
In this context, Sudanese writer and researcher Abbas Saleh, who is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, told The New Arab that Uganda's potential participation in the proposed international force for the Gaza Strip reflects a renewed predicament facing the African Union.
Decisions and positions adopted by the continental organisation often appear non-binding on member states, which may adopt unilateral policies that conflict with the union's collective positions.
"Despite the clear positions adopted by the African Union on the Palestinian cause, its rejection of Israeli violations and its repeated calls for an end to the war and the protection of civilians, the involvement of some member states in international security arrangements linked to Gaza could weaken the unity of the African position and expose the organisation's limited ability to turn its political positions into practical commitments by its members," he pointed out.
According to Saleh, Uganda is among the countries whose name has for years been associated with a broad security and military role in Africa, as well as close relations with Western powers, particularly in the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa.
He explained that this role "has given it a prominent position in several regional security issues but has at times made its foreign policy a subject of debate over the extent to which its decisions are independent of the calculations of international powers".
"The Ugandan move is significant beyond the participation of a single country, as it could set a precedent encouraging other countries that had been hesitant or reluctant to join the proposed international force, particularly if they are provided with appropriate political and security guarantees or international incentives," Saleh opined.
He stressed that participation in a military mission inside Gaza carries significant risks, given the complexities of the security and political situation, continuing disagreements over the future of the territory and governance and security arrangements, and the sensitivity surrounding the presence of foreign forces in the Palestinian territories.
"Uganda's move places the African Union before a difficult test: how can the organisation maintain a unified African position on the Palestinian cause while each member state has broad scope to make its foreign and security decisions independently?" he added. "The union's ability to deal with these contradictions could be an important indicator of the effectiveness of its political positions, not only towards Palestine, but also towards international crises affecting the continent and the interests of its countries."
Contradictions, differences
Meanwhile, researcher on Sahel and Sahara affairs Mohamed Torshin told The New Arab that the participation of Ugandan forces in the peace process in Gaza clearly reflects the scale of contradictions within the African Union and its limited ability to impose or implement decisions taken collectively, whether at the level of the AU Commission, the Peace and Security Council or the General Assembly.
Although African Union decisions and collective positions are supposed to form a common political framework for member states, the Ugandan position, along with other previous cases, reveals clear differences in the positions of African countries towards several sensitive regional and international issues.
In many cases, these differences push some countries or regional blocs to adopt policies and approaches that conflict with the union's collective position.
According to Torshin, the repercussions are not limited to a particular issue but extend to the effectiveness of African decision-making in general.
When a member state, in his view, adopts a position that clearly contradicts the union's collective position, this weakens the organisation's ability to present itself as a unified political actor and limits its ability to exercise diplomatic influence on issues requiring a coherent continental position.
In this context, Torshin noted that the repetition of such cases could widen the gap between decisions issued by African Union institutions and the policies pursued by some member states at the national level.
"This would gradually weaken the ability of the AU Commission and its political bodies to turn collective positions and decisions into effective and binding policies, making African decision-making more vulnerable to fragmentation and differences between countries and regional blocs," he added.
Torshin pointed out that the lack of protocol and political coordination between different African countries, ministries and institutions, and the absence of unified positions and decisions on common issues, could create space for international parties with interests and programmes in Africa to deal with countries individually and implement their policies and projects according to their own interests, away from the collective frameworks and decisions of the African Union.
He argued that "as this divergence and the multiplicity of positions within the continental organisation continue, international powers may find themselves with greater room to manoeuvre and negotiate with African countries bilaterally, gradually weakening the union's ability to formulate and defend a unified African agenda".
"In the long term, the continuation of this fragmentation could affect the future of African integration, making the implementation of continental policies and projects more closely tied to the interests of countries and external partners, and less subject to the collective vision that the union is supposed to represent," Torshin warned.

articles.title: Zelensky on Coalition of the Willing summit: Ukraine to receive new support packages, air defense and funding for drones

Zelensky on Coalition of the Willing summit: Ukraine to receive new support packages, air defense and funding for drones

articles.body:
Sahin Demir
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Israeli army forces carried out an airstrike and artillery shelling in southern Lebanon early Tuesday, and erected new earth barriers in the area, in the latest violation of a US-mediated framework agreement, Lebanese media reported.
Israeli warplanes struck the course of the Litani River below the Deir Mar Mima monastery in the town of Deir Mimas at around 4 am local time (0100GMT), according to Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA).
Separately, the town of Markaba in the Marjayoun district came under Israeli artillery shelling as Israeli military vehicles were seen moving in the town, the agency said.
NNA also reported that Israeli forces stationed in Kfar Kila and Tall al-Nahhas erected an earth barrier at the Deir Mimas-Burj al-Muluk-Kfar Kila junction toward Tall al-Nahhas, around 150 meters (492 feet) from inhabited homes in Burj al-Muluk.
Israeli forces erected another earth barrier at the Deir Mimas-Burj al-Muluk-Houra junction toward the Houra area, it added.
The violations come amid continuing tensions between Israel and Lebanon following the outbreak of a new round of hostilities on March 2.
Israel has launched extensive attacks on Lebanon since March 2, claiming they targeted Hezbollah, while the group responded with attacks against Israel, effectively ending the ceasefire that had been in place since November 2024.
US-led diplomatic efforts led to the signing of a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon in June, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army there and the disarmament of armed groups.
